The Budget Lab at Yale, which monitors the impact of US government policy on the economy, says it anticipates seeing marginal increases in furnishing and other household equipment for Americans largely due to tariffs on lumber and other materials.
There may not be a material impact on alcohol prices, but it's clear the trade war has had an impact on Canadians' choice of drink.
Many provinces in the country banned US alcohol sales last year in response to previous tariffs, with the American wine and spirits industry saying exports to the country dropped more than 70%.
Carney asked the provinces to restore US alcohol to the shelves during trade talks, but now that they have collapsed, it's likely the ban will return.
Saunders says there's been a big push to "buy Canadian" from politicians and it has been successful when it comes to the strong stuff.
"That's really had an impact on the American alcohol industry," he adds.

Saskatchewan and Alberta are ​the only provinces that still sell ​American alcohol, but the former has announced its own 50% charge on US imported booze, set to kick in on 8 September, when the wider Canadian tariffs do.
While tariffs can end up hitting consumers in the pocket, there are other impacts on households.

Import taxes can complicate trade for businesses that have cross-border supply. As well as the higher costs, the uncertainty created by the trade war could put off investment plans and stunt job creation.
Saunders suggests the biggest impact on households may not just be through prices, but job losses instead.

"If you're, let's say, a bespoke furniture producer in BC [British Columbia], you're now facing a 50% tariff on your exports to the US - that could really shut the business down. I think that would be more the direct impact on households as opposed to these retaliatory measures."

Canada's forest industry employs almost 200,000 people and has called on the government to boost domestic demand through federal housing programs to make greater use of Canadian wood, though it admits "no support package can replace reliable access to our largest export market".

When it comes to US, consumers are unlikely to see much of a difference in terms of the cost of living as result of this latest battle with Canada, but frictions to trade can have longer-term economic impacts.

Such tensions also feed into concerns over the free-trade agreement between Canada, the US and Mexico, known as the USMCA. Both Canada and Mexico have said they want the USMCA extended for another 16 years, but the US has said it will not renew in its current form.
Despite the deal remaining operational, tariffs risk putting off talks in the near future, creating more uncertainty for cross-border trade.

John Iselin, associate director at the Budget Lab at Yale, estimates the cost will only be about $3 per American household on average, but when taking into account Trump's wider trade war with the rest of the world, and particularly China, the added costs rise to about $1,000 for the average family.

"It's hard to view this particular instance with Canada in isolation because we've had similar interactions with a range of other countries, all of which makes doing business harder. It's just another in a series of tariff shocks."

articles.title: B.C. NDP MLA Joan Phillip dead at 74
articles.summary: Joan Phillip, the NDP MLA for Vancouver-Strathcona and wife of Union of British Columbia Indian Chiefs (UBCIC) Grand Chief Stewart Phillip, has died.

image.caption: Joan Phillip, the MLA for Vancouver-Strathcona, has died, the Union of British Columbia Indian Chiefs said Friday. (BC NDP)

blocks.text: British Columbia·Breaking
Joan Phillip, the NDP MLA for Vancouver-Strathcona and wife of Union of British Columbia Indian Chiefs (UBCIC) Grand Chief Stewart Phillip, has died.
The Union of British Columbia Indian Chiefs says Phillip died Friday afternoon
The UBCIC released a statement saying Phillip, also known as Amshen, died peacefully Friday afternoon.
She was 74. While an exact cause of death was not stated, the UBCIC asked people donate to the B.C. Cancer Society in lieu of sending flowers.
Phillip was surrounded by her family at the time, according to the statement.
"Joan passed away peacefully this afternoon, surrounded by the love of her life," the UBCIC said.

British Columbia lost a powerful and respected leader when Joan Amshen Phillip died earlier today. Our caucus and staff are grieving alongside her family and so many others who knew and loved her. pic.twitter.com/WH6KGWvZjz—Dave_Eby
B.C. Premier David Eby said the NDP caucus and staff are grieving alongside Phillip’s family.
"British Columbia lost a powerful and respected leader when Joan Amshen Phillip died earlier today," said Eby in a written statement.
Earlier this year, Eby said that Phillip was "very ill" and that her colleagues were all praying for her.
He called Phillip a "hugely respected member of many communities" and a "loved and valued" colleague of those in the legislature from across party lines.
Phillip, an Indigenous leader, was credited by Eby as one of the reasons why the NDP halted its plans to suspend sections of the Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples Act, or DRIPA.
She was first elected in Vancouver in a 2023 byelection, and won again in B.C.'s general election the following year.
More to come.
With files from The Canadian Press

articles.title: [Vantage Point] PROCAP: How a scam came to look legitimate
articles.summary: A look at how an apparently well-organized, cross-border operation combined gaming, cryptocurrency, referral networks, purported insurance, technology, international events, prominent personalities,…

blocks.text: A look at how an apparently well-organized, cross-border operation combined gaming, cryptocurrency, referral networks, purported insurance, technology, international events, prominent personalities, and genuine early payouts to manufacture credibility on an extraordinary scale

items: ProCap International (PROCAP) successfully deceived sophisticated individuals, including businessmen and politicians, by creating a facade of legitimacy and credibility, despite being identified as a Ponzi scheme by regulators.

The operation attracted participants through promises of high returns, purported insurance, and social proof from prominent figures, which obscured the underlying fraudulent nature of the investment scheme.

As withdrawals began to halt and legal actions were initiated against its operators, the complexity of the fraud revealed that even educated and wealthy individuals are not immune to sophisticated scams that exploit trust and credibility.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

ProCap did not become believable by targeting only the gullible. It manufactured credibility so effectively that businessmen, academics, lawyers and even former justice secretary Vitaliano Aguirre II appeared persuaded that nothing was amiss.
The most dangerous scams are not those that look like scams. They are those that look legitimate, behave legitimately and, for a surprisingly long time, pay people as promised.

PROCAP International (PROCAP) may be one of the more extraordinary examples because among those drawn into its orbit were precisely the people we normally assume should know better: businessmen, politicians, lawyers, academics and other sophisticated Filipinos accustomed to making intelligent decisions involving money.

And who wouldn’t be reassured when even former justice secretary Vitaliano Aguirre II appeared convinced nothing was amiss? Aguirre attended an October 2023 PROCAP gathering at a Makati hotel raided by police, who arrested 20 people.

blocks.caption: INVESTMENT SCAM? Marketing firm ProCap International holds a ‘Galaxy Night’ at the Dusit Thani Hotel in Makati on October 15, 2023, prior to an “entrapment operation” leading to the arrest of 20 people related to the company. Courtesy of Presidential Anti-Organized Crime Commission

blocks.text: The Philippine National Police (PNP) Criminal Investigation and Detection Group (CIDG) identified him as one of the company’s lawyers, while GMA News reported that Aguirre “insisted that there was nothing wrong with the company’s transactions.” (READ: Procap denies scam allegations as SEC reiterates firm’s illegal activities)

Israelito “Bobbet” P. Torreon, a prominent trial lawyer and academician, approached us with documents and an insider’s account of how PROCAP operated. He represents one of its biggest alleged victims, whose identity I am deliberately withholding because this story is not about her. What interests me is how an operation promising returns that should have triggered alarm bells became sufficiently believable to attract people nobody would ordinarily describe as gullible.

The Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) said in October 2023 that PROCAP offered investment contracts disguised as gaming packages ranging from about P73,000 to P4.3 million, promising returns of 6% to 42% monthly. Participants supposedly followed a prescribed gaming formula, while a “capital protection insurance” mechanism purportedly protected their money after successive losing predictions.

Forty-two percent monthly should ordinarily have ended the conversation. But PROCAP had an extraordinarily persuasive answer: people were getting paid. According to Torreon, participants funded gaming accounts using payments converted into USDT or Tether, a stablecoin pegged to the US dollar. Dashboards displayed daily winnings, supposedly split 50-50 between PROCAP and the player, and winnings initially could be withdrawn the following day.

That shifts the psychology completely. Imagine a trusted friend showing you his account, playing and successfully withdrawing his winnings. You try it yourself and get paid. At that point PROCAP no longer needs to convince you its system works; your own experience seems to prove it. Add purported insurance, cryptocurrency technology and a dashboard that Torreon says generated an insurance policy whenever an account was opened, and risk itself appeared to have been engineered away.

Hong Kong’s Securities and Futures Commission independently warned in April 2024 about substantially the same proposition—packages costing 1,235 to 74,000 USDT, purported capital insurance, referral incentives and monthly returns of 6% to 42%.
Then came social proof. Torreon’s documents describe a lavish Dubai event featuring raffles for Rolls-Royce, Bentley, Mercedes-Benz and BMW vehicles, gold bars and luxury watches.

Businessmen, lawyers, politicians, media personalities and other prominent people participated. Each layer answered another doubt: the capital was supposedly insured, withdrawals proved the money was real, prominent participants supplied credibility and dashboards provided technological reassurance. PROCAP’s apparent genius was the industrialization of trust.

The SEC eventually reached a very different conclusion. It revoked PROCAP International’s corporate registration and found characteristics of a Ponzi scheme, where money from newer participants finances payments to those who entered earlier. (READ: From robots to beef pares: The classic Ponzi scheme is still scamming Filipinos)

blocks.caption: How I recovered the money I invested in MFT

blocks.text: If that characterization correctly describes PROCAP’s economic machinery, the successful withdrawals that convinced investors of its legitimacy were not proof of sustainability. They were precisely what enabled the operation to expand.

Then the machinery apparently began breaking down. Torreon says withdrawals stopped being released normally in December 2024. Participants were told that Singaporean PROCAP figure James Teo had been jailed in China and that his absence prevented access to funds because he supposedly controlled one of three security keys needed for blockchain transactions.
Torreon says his client’s group checked Teo’s whereabouts through the Singapore embassy and, by January 2024, filed a criminal case against alleged foreign PROCAP operators.

Another major victim filed separately in Santa Rosa, Laguna the following month. Torreon says both cases eventually reached court, producing non-bailable arrest warrants that were subsequently used in seeking Interpol Red Notices against the foreign respondents. Interpol Red Notice is a global request by International Police Criminal Organization to law enforcement agencies worldwide to locate and provisionally arrest a person pending extradition, surrender or similar legal action.

That chronology is important because it complicates what happened next. In May 2025, another lawyer representing six alleged victims publicly announced a P42-billion large-scale estafa complaint and included members of the family Torreon represents among those accused.

Torreon disputes both their alleged role and the headline amount, pointing out that documents he provided show the six complainants’ own claimed placements were below P20 million. The P42-billion figure therefore should be treated for what it presently is: an allegation in a complaint, not a judicial determination of actual losses or criminal liability as claimed by the lawyer/vlogger.

More significantly, Torreon argues that his client had already gone after the alleged foreign operators more than a year earlier since January 2025 and helped pursue the warrants and Red Notices against them.

That does not by itself settle who ultimately bears responsibility; those are questions for prosecutors and the courts. But it is a material part of the chronology and demonstrates why we should distinguish allegations against particular Filipino participants from facts already established by regulators.

What regulators have established is serious enough. The SEC acted against PROCAP’s investment solicitation, while Hong Kong authorities separately warned investors about substantially the same products.

What deserves further investigation is how an apparently well-organized, cross-border operation combined gaming, cryptocurrency, referral networks, purported insurance, technology, international events, prominent personalities and genuine early payouts to manufacture credibility on an extraordinary scale.
PROCAP’s lesson therefore is not that foolish people chased impossible riches. That explanation is convenient but intellectually lazy.

A sophisticated investor is not immune from fraud merely because he is educated, wealthy, politically connected or surrounded by lawyers. A sophisticated fraud understands precisely what sophisticated people demand before surrendering their money: evidence, credibility, professional validation, successful transactions, and people they trust.
PROCAP apparently supplied them all. Perhaps that is the darkest triumph of a well-organized financial fraud: it never asks intelligent people to swallow an absurdity whole.

It buries the lie beneath payouts, dashboards, prominent names and every reassuring sign of legitimacy—until doubt feels foolish, belief feels rational and, one day, the screen still shows a fortune, but the money is gone. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Canada poaches dozens of top US researchers for its universities
articles.summary: Lured by millions of new research funding from the Carney government, 48 US researchers in fields like climate and medicine will soon be moving north.

blocks.text: Canada is hiring dozens of researchers away from US universities, including top research institutions such as Harvard as its relationship with its neighbour continues to sour.

More than three-fourths of the 64 professors who are moving to Canada from around the world will come from the US. Under a new government programme, they'll receive funding from a pool of C$504m ($362m; £268m) for research in fields such as climate change and medicine.
US President Donald Trump's administration has accused universities of being dominated by left-wing ideology and diversity policies, and of failing to tackle alleged campus antisemitism.
The BBC contacted the White House and US Department of Education.

The administration has also frozen federal research grants for many different institutions and groups that they have argued are wasteful, external. That uncertainty is helping lure researchers elsewhere.
Meanwhile, Canada is asserting itself more on the global stage while it pushes back against the US in their escalating trade war, which reached a major turning point over tariffs recently.
One climate researcher told the BBC he was relocating to Canada in part because his work in the US had become more difficult in recent years.

Seth Guikema, a climate resiliency researcher at the University of Michigan and one of the 48 US researchers relocating to Canada, said he decided to approach Canadian institutions last year in search of opportunities.

"The funding environment in the US for anything related to climate and resilience has become challenging," Guikema said. "I was looking for a good intellectual home where I could have practical impact."
Over the next eight years, Guikema said he would use C$8m to research tools for better preparing for natural hazards, like storms and wildfires, at the University of Western Ontario.
The University of Michigan, his former employer, declined to comment.
Canada's Industry Minister Melanie Joly said on Thursday the government was "very glad that these fantastic professors are coming".

Asked if the programme was poaching US talent and whether it could be viewed by the Trump administration as an escalation of the US-Canada trade war, she said on Thursday: "The US administration is taking its own decisions and we're taking ours."
Some of the researchers chosen for the programme, like Guikema, were born and raised in the US. Others are Canadians who worked abroad and are now returning home.

Peter Caravan, who worked for two decades as a biopharmaceutical researcher and professor at Massachusetts General Hospital and Harvard Medical School, appeared emotional at a Thursday news conference announcing the research appointments.
Caravan is researching how illnesses like cancers and chronic diseases can be better detected - work that will now be done out of the University of British Columbia in Vancouver.
Steven Lamy, a professor of International Relations at the University of Southern California, argued that major grant agencies "have been cut and politicised" by the current US administration.
"All of a sudden employment offers from external universities are attractive," he said.
Stephanie Burt, an English professor at Harvard University, believed the funding cuts were "a generational disaster for science and scientists".
She told the BBC that Canada had offered a "far more welcoming environment" for academics.
US universities are still among the top ranked in the world, according to QS Universities Rankings, with the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT), Stanford and Harvard in the top five.
Lynn Pasquerella, the president of the American Association of Colleges and Universities, said institutions feel "helpless" in the face of federal and state cuts.
The deeper concern, she added, "is not the short-term brain drain", but "the possibility that the US could become less attractive as a place to pursue knowledge".

articles.title: Controversial plans for a Daniel Andrews sculpture officially scrapped by Victorian government
articles.summary:
The $134,000 cost of the statue of the former Victorian premier has been heavily criticised by the Liberal opposition

  • Get our

blocks.text: The Carroll government in Victoria has cancelled controversial plans for a statue of former Labor premier Daniel Andrews.
Work began in May on the statue commemorating the former premier’s more than 3,000 days in office, as part of a 1999 policy recognising long-serving Victorian premiers.

But the premier, Ben Carroll, announced an end to the Kennett government policy on Saturday, appointing an independent panel to review how Victoria commemorates officials with statues and state services.
He directed work on the Andrews statue to cease.
“We are grateful to former premiers for their service. But gratitude does not require a taxpayer-funded statue,” Carroll said.
“I respect your money. That means being careful and deliberate about how government spends it.”

The policy automatically recognising long-serving Victorian premiers with a statue on Treasury Place was introduced ahead of the 1999 state election by then-premier Jeff Kennett. Kennett himself fell short of the milestone.

The “independent and bipartisan” panel will make recommendations about the future state funerals and memorial services. The statue contract will not be cancelled, instead the panel will select an alternative subject and location for the commissioned work.
The $134,000 cost of the planned statue of Andrews has been heavily criticised by the Liberal opposition.
“If we come to government we will not allow that statue to proceed,” the opposition leader, Jess Wilson, said on 30 July.
“Victorians are fed up with Labor’s waste – that’s why it’s time for a Government that treats your money with respect,” she wrote in a social media post.
Andrews was premier of Victoria from 4 December 2014 to 27 September 2023.

In May, the state government confirmed Meridian Sculpture, the company that created the statues of the other four Victorian premiers who reached the milestone, was selected after a standard procurement process.

At the time, a Victorian government spokesperson said: “Daniel Andrews led Victoria through some of its toughest moments and never stopped fighting for working people. Under a policy introduced by the Kennett government, Victorian premiers who serve more than 3,000 days in office are recognised with a statue along Treasury Place in honour of their service to the state.”

articles.title: De Lima: Meta sharing info with gov’t OK as long as it’s vs threats
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — There is no issue with Meta’s decision to share with the Philippine government the information of its users as long as it is in the context of fighting threats and not…

blocks.caption: House prosecutor and Mamamayang Liberal party-list Representative Leila de Lima —Inquirer photo/Niño Jesus Orbeta

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — There is no issue with Meta’s decision to share with the Philippine government the information of its users as long as it is in the context of fighting threats and not conducting surveillance, human rights advocate and Mamamayang Liberal party-list Rep. Leila de Lima said on Friday.

De Lima, in a statement, said that Meta’s decision to cooperate with local authorities in terms of identifying potential threats, as relayed by Senator Risa Hontiveros, is a welcome development, especially for her since she is one of the lawmakers who have been pushing for a bill that would protect minors from harms brought by the internet.

“As one of the principal authors of (the proposed) Child Online Safety and Protection Act in the House of Representatives, this is a crucial step toward making social media safer for our children,” she said.

“As I said, we must not be reactive but relentless in protecting our children. This safeguard should have been put in place long ago, especially since their platform has been used for online threats, child abuse, grooming, exploitation and sexual extortion schemes, among other heinous crimes,” she added.

Hontiveros on Friday said that a Philippine delegation was able to elicit a commitment from Meta, which owns and manages social media sites Facebook, Instagram, and Threads, along with other messaging apps, to provide authorities important information should they spot a possible threat to children.

While it is good news, De Lima said it must be clear that the purpose of this user data sharing is to fight threats brought by violent social media content, and not to profile individuals expressing legitimate dissent.
“Also, let us be clear: Our purpose should be to shrink the world of predators by enabling us to pursue them across borders, not to shrink our democratic space,” she said.

“Data sharing must be commensurate with the intent or scope of data to be released so as not to open the gate to state surveillance of legitimate criticism and the weaponization of the law,” De Lima explained.

Currently, there is strong support from different branches of the government towards a social media ban for children. At Thursday’s hearing of the House committee on appropriations, Interior Secretary Jonvic Remulla said he agrees with the proposed social media ban, backing suggestions to restrict it for users aged 14 and below.
“I am in total agreement with the ban,” Remulla told lawmakers. “I would prefer 14-years-old and below that they be banned or restricted hours of use.”
Then on Wednesday, the Senate committee on public information and mass media endorsed a bill seeking to set 16 years old as the minimum age for social media use.

Both moves came amid fears that unrestricted social media use may have led students behind the school shooting incidents at the San Jose National High School in Tacloban City last June 22 and the Ateneo de Zamboanga University in Zamboanga City last August 18 to do these actions.
Three students were killed during the Tacloban shooting, while two, including the gunman, were confirmed dead after the incident at Ateneo de Zamboanga University.
There is a belief that the perpetrators in both incidents were supposedly exposed to violent content online.

But aside from just curbing violence in campuses, De Lima said the cooperation should be “maximized” and include other issues such as the proliferation of fake news, disinformation and misinformation campaigns—matters that the lawmaker said also pose a threat to the country’s sovereignty and peace and order situation.

“This coordination should also be maximized to combat fake news and disinformation, which pose real and urgent threats to our sovereignty, peace and order, national security, healthcare, electoral and justice systems, and civil liberties,” she said.
“Law enforcement must go after abusers and dismantle networks and coordinated disinformation campaigns that use troll farms and similar infrastructure to sow distrust and negativism,” she added.

Malacañang on Thursday said there is no immediate need to ban Facebook in the Philippines after the social media giant showed willingness to respond to government requests to remove fake news and violent content.

The possibility of restricting access to other social media platforms and other online gaming apps, however, remains should they fail to regulate content that could influence the youth to engage in violent behavior and the proliferation of misinformation and disinformation.
Two medical groups have also warned against the unsupervised use of social media by children aged 16 years old and below, saying that it poses risks to a child’s mental health and development.

In a statement on Facebook on Friday, the Philippine Pediatric Society (PPS) said it does not recommend social media use among children 16 and below. Should they be given access, the group said children should not be allowed to use social media independently. /cb

blocks.text: Donald Trump announced Friday a new US oil agreement with Venezuela’s interim president Delcy Rodríguez, saying the US will have “majority” control of 65bn barrels of proven oil reserves.

The terms of the agreement remain to be seen, but the US president said on his social-media platform that it had been brokered “through a partnership with ⁠private business” by his secretary of state, Marco Rubio, and defense secretary, Pete Hegseth.
The administration, Trump wrote, has “secured majority U.S. control of more ​than 65 BILLION ‌BARRELS of proven Oil ‌Reserves in Venezuela, at no cost to the ‌American Taxpayer”.
Trump said the agreement would more than double American oil reserves.
“This deal is a huge win for both the American and Venezuelan people,” Rubio wrote on social media.
Trump’s announcement provided few details on the structure of the agreement, the fields or companies involved, or how the US would exercise majority control over the ⁠reserves.
Venezuela has an estimated 303bn barrels of proven oil reserves, the world’s largest.

Since the US captured and removed former Venezuelan president Nicolás Maduro from power in January, Washington has been trying ‌to secure a stable flow of Venezuelan crude oil for US refineries while promoting American investment ​into the Opec country’s deteriorated energy industry, which produces 1.25m barrels per day of crude.
Trump is under pressure before November’s midterm elections over rising gasoline prices, ​which could ​be eased through ​cheaper oil supplies and expanded output.
The US ​also has ‌been looking ​for solutions ​to replenish its strategic petroleum reserve, the oil stockpile, including the possibility of crude swaps with US producers.

Earlier this week, the Wall Street Journal reported that the Trump administration was “in advanced talks with Venezuela for the U.S. to take a direct stake in more than a dozen oilfields that house nearly one-third of the country’s massive energy reserves”. Axios also reported on the negotiations, quoting a US official who claimed the deal would be “massive”.
The discussion was reportedly over a US stake in Venezuela’s most promising oil-and-gasfields, with some 90bn barrels of proven reserves.
The reports caused unease and anger among members of Venezuela’s opposition, who are already up in arms about Trump’s failure to bring about genuine political change after capturing Maduro.

“It’s a land grab – a massive land grab,” said one well-known opposition figure who asked not to be named because of the sensitivities of criticizing the US. “It’s revolting because this is not the United States one would have [expected]. This is not the United States of the Marshall plan. This is a rapacious, mafioso United States.”
The announcement comes as Chevron and other US energy companies are expected to sign a deal next week investing billions in Venezuela’s oil fields, according to the Journal.
Tom Phillips and Reuters contributed reporting

articles.summary: U.S. President Donald Trump on Friday said the U.S. has entered an agreement with Venezuela to take control of 65 billion barrels of the South American country's oil reserves.

image.caption: U.S. President Donald Trump is seen at the Johnson Space Center's Mission Control Center in Houston on Friday. (Mark Schiefelbein/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: World
U.S. President Donald Trump on Friday said the U.S. has entered an agreement with Venezuela to take control of 65 billion barrels of the South American country's oil reserves.
U.S. president touts agreement as 'biggest oil deal in world history'
Trump in a social media post announced the agreement he said was negotiated by Secretary of State Marco Rubio, Secretary of War Pete Hegseth and Venezuela's interim President Delcy Rodriguez.
"The United States of America has just entered into an Agreement with the Country of Venezuela on, THE BIGGEST OIL DEAL IN WORLD HISTORY!" Trump wrote.

The announcement of the deal comes nearly nine months after the U.S. military at Trump's direction carried out an operation to capture Venezuela's president Nicolás Maduro and spirit him to the United States to face federal narcoterrorism and drug trafficking charges.
Trump faces mounting pressure to address high gas prices as the war in Iran reaches a six-month milestone with no conclusion in sight.
The U.S. has tapped its strategic petroleum reserves, which in early August fell below 300 million barrels, down by more than 100 million barrels since the start of 2026.

items: Venezuela's collapse, Trump's military buildup and Maduro's capture: How did we get here?
Who is Nicolás Maduro, Venezuela's recently captured president?

blocks.text: In the days following Maduro's ouster in January, Trump floated the idea of U.S. oil companies returning to Venezuela to tap its oil reserves.

Trump has argued that Venezuela stole U.S. oil when former Venezuelan president Hugo Chavez moved decades ago to nationalize hundreds of foreign-owned assets, including those owned by American oil companies.
Venezuela has one of the largest oil reserves in the world, with an estimated 303 billion barrels of crude oil in the ground.
That's about 17 per cent of the world's supply, according to the U.S. Energy Information Administration.
Unlike other parts of the world, where geologists have to search for untapped oil, the reserves under Venezuela's soil are largely mapped and known, experts say.
But because of dilapidated infrastructure, the country only produces about 1 per cent of the world's oil.

articles.title: Philippines, UK eye expanded space cooperation, satellite to boost disaster response
articles.summary: The Philippines and the United Kingdom are looking to deepen cooperation in space science and technology, satellite data, artificial intelligence (AI), and innovation, as the two countries prepare…

blocks.text: The Philippines and the United Kingdom are looking to deepen cooperation in space science and technology, satellite data, artificial intelligence (AI), and innovation, as the two countries prepare for the launch of the Multispectral Unit for Land Assessment (MULA) satellite.

Philippine Space Agency (PhilSA) Acting Director General Dr. Gay Jane Perez met with United Kingdom Trade Commissioner Martin Kent to discuss MULA's upcoming launch and future opportunities to strengthen bilateral cooperation in space technology applications, according to posts by the British Embassy in the Philippines and PhilSA.
The British Embassy said MULA, developed in partnership with the United Kingdom, would support disaster response, agriculture, and environmental monitoring across the Philippines.

The satellite is expected to give the Philippines greater capacity to use Earth observation data for disaster risk reduction and management, as well as for monitoring land, resources, and environmental conditions.
PhilSA has said MULA will provide data for agriculture, maritime monitoring, disaster risk reduction and management, and national security applications.

The agency has also cited the importance of satellite data in disaster operations, including the production of maps showing landslide and earthquake damage, oil spills, burned areas, and flood extents for government disaster response agencies and local governments.

PhilSA previously said MULA's higher-resolution imaging capability would allow the country to better monitor terrestrial ecosystems, land and marine resources, agricultural activity, and environmental conditions for more proactive disaster management and mitigation.
“From Earth observation to space innovation, the UK and the Philippines are reaching new heights together,” the British Embassy said.
Possible 2027 launch

MULA, described by PhilSA as the country's most advanced satellite to date, is now fully built and undergoing space environment testing in the United Kingdom to verify that it meets technical and mission-assurance requirements.

During the ninth meeting of the Philippine Space Council in June, Perez reported that MULA could be launched in April 2027 aboard SpaceX's Transporter-20, although PhilSA stressed that the development schedule could still change depending on the results of testing.

The satellite will carry a TrueColour camera capable of producing 5-meter-resolution images, as well as Automatic Identification System and Automatic Dependent Surveillance-Broadcast payloads for detecting and tracking ships and aircraft.
“As MULA paves the way for a new era of capability, the UK looks forward to deepening its partnership with PhilSA and advancing even more ambitious space collaborations,” the British Embassy said.
UK partnership

The UK-Philippines space partnership has been closely linked to MULA's development, with Filipino engineers receiving satellite-development training and hands-on experience from Surrey Satellite Technology Ltd. (SSTL) in the United Kingdom.
PhilSA said most MULA engineers have completed intensive know-how transfer and hands-on training with SSTL, allowing them to apply advanced satellite engineering expertise in the Philippines.

The agency also previously reported that a UK trade envoy met with PhilSA and MULA engineers in 2022 to discuss the satellite project and opportunities to build more sovereign Philippine satellites in the future.

PhilSA's June report said the Philippine Space Council had approved the development of a MULA constellation as a national priority, allowing follow-on satellites to be developed and integrated domestically to ensure more continuous access to Earth-observation data.
PhilSA said the initiative would help build a Philippine space industry and establish a nationally owned and operated Earth-observation capability for the country's strategic requirements.

blocks.text: US President Donald Trump said on Friday the US had reached a deal to take control of Venezuela's vast oil reserves.
He said the deal was negotiated by Secretary of State Marco Rubio, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and Venezuelan interim President Delcy Rodriguez.
"The United States of America has just entered into an agreement with the country of Venezuela on, THE BIGGEST OIL DEAL IN WORLD HISTORY!" Trump wrote on his Truth Social platform.

Rubio said the deal would see $100 billion (€86 billion) of private investment flow into Venezuela.
"This deal is a huge win for both the American and Venezuelan people," he said.
The agreement promises to more-than-double US oil reserves.
The world's largest oil reserves

The deal comes nearly nine months after US forces deposed and kidnapped Venezuelan leader Nicolas Maduro. He is now detained in New York City, where he faces federal narcoterrorism and drug trafficking charges.
Since then, and under intense pressure, Rodriguez has moved to open up Venezuela's oil sector to American investment.

Venezuela has the world's largest proven oil reserves totaling 303 billion barrels. But production has long lagged behind other major oil producing countries due to chronic mismanagement, decaying infrastructure and sanctions.

articles.title: Socmed ban for 14 and below backed amid fears of online drug trade
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — A lawmaker has thrown his support behind proposals to restrict social media use for children aged 14 and below amid fears that the internet is being used by drug syndicates to…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — A lawmaker has thrown his support behind proposals to restrict social media use for children aged 14 and below amid fears that the internet is being used by drug syndicates to recruit young people and even engage in drug trade through coded communication.

In a statement on Friday, Las Piñas Rep. Mark Anthony Santos said he backs the proposal that would ban children from accessing social media—which was also supported by Interior Secretary Jonvic Remulla, as he stated during the House of Representatives’ committee on appropriations budget briefing on the proposed 2027 budget of the Department of the Interior and Local Government (DILG).
Santos, chairperson of the House committee on dangerous drugs, did not present data or actual incidents, but he claimed that drug syndicates are now using social media to recruit children.

“Our children are among the most vulnerable targets in the digital world. We cannot allow drug syndicates to use social media as a hunting ground to recruit, manipulate and expose young people to illegal drugs,” he said.

“Technology has made it easier for criminals to reach potential victims. A young person can be targeted, manipulated and eventually introduced to illegal drugs without realizing that he or she is already being drawn into a criminal network,” he added.
During the appropriations committee hearing on Thursday, Remulla said he agrees with the proposed social media ban, backing suggestions to restrict it for users aged 14 and below.
“I am in total agreement with the ban,” Remulla told lawmakers. “I would prefer 14-years-old and below that they be banned or restricted hours of use.”
Then on Wednesday, the Senate committee on public information and mass media endorsed a bill seeking to set 16 years old as the minimum age for social media use.

Both moves came amid fears that unrestricted social media use may have led students behind the school shooting incidents at the San Jose National High School in Tacloban City last June 22 and the Ateneo de Zamboanga University in Zamboanga City last August 18 to do these actions.
Three students were killed during the Tacloban shooting, while two, including the gunman, were confirmed dead after the incident at Ateneo de Zamboanga University.
There is a belief that the perpetrators in both incidents were supposedly exposed to violent content online.
But Santos said that aside from violent content, the Philippines and other countries have faced problems regarding young children being recruited towards scrupulous activities, including drug trade.

Although social media platforms prohibit the sale and promotion of illegal drugs, Santos said young users could still encounter drug dealers through online accounts, private messages, and encrypted or otherwise less-visible digital channels.
Drug enforcement authorities, he added, have reported drug-related activities taking place across major online platforms, particularly messaging applications widely used in the Philippines.

“The fight against illegal drugs should not be limited to the streets. We must also confront the new methods being used by drug syndicates in cyberspace,” Santos added. —WITH REPORTS FROM RENDELL IVAN MANUEL, TRAINEE

articles.title: AFP witnesses to clarify certifications on DepEd CF liquidation
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — Two military officers expected before the Senate impeachment court can help explain why Armed Forces of the Philippines (AFP) certifications were used in Department of Education…

blocks.caption: House Deputy Speaker Paolo Ortega V —Photo from Radyo Pilipinas/Facebook

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — Two military officers expected before the Senate impeachment court can help explain why Armed Forces of the Philippines (AFP) certifications were used in Department of Education confidential-fund records even though the signatories previously said they did not know that purpose, House prosecution spokespersons said Friday.

Retired Col. Manaros Boransing II and Col. Magtangol Panopio are scheduled as prosecution witnesses. Their certifications figured in DepEd’s response to audit findings regarding its 2023 confidential fund expenses while Vice President Sara Duterte was still the education secretary.

Deputy Speaker Paolo Ortega V of La Union said their testimony should connect details left open by earlier witnesses. “Matatahi na yung buong kuwento, kumbaga,” he said during the prosecution’s August 28 online press conference.
“Makikita natin kung paano ginastos, saan napunta, ba’t walang resibo, ba’t walang additional information tungkol sa nagamit,” Ortega said. “We will shed some light on these topics.”

House impeachment team adviser and spokesperson Ace Barbers said the hearing should also protect the military’s institutional neutrality. “Ang Armed Forces of the Philippines ay isang organisasyon na hindi dapat na-involve sa politika,” he said.
The testimony should show whether military officers knowingly took part in the fund process or whether their signatures were used without a full explanation of the documents’ purpose.

“Kung sila ay lalabas na ginamit sa anumang personal na layunin ng ilang mga politiko, may dapat pananagutan,” Barbers said. He added that accountability is also required if the officers were drawn into the transaction without their knowledge.

Barbers said the certifications matter because they may have been used to answer an audit question and support a public-fund liquidation. He declined to predict the witnesses’ testimony, saying the public should watch how the documents are explained in court.
The larger principle is simple, he said: “They should remain apolitical; they should remain neutral.”
Ortega said distributing confidential fund cash was outside the security officers’ assigned role. “Hindi po nila trabaho iyan, kumuha ng pera at ipamigay yung mga pera na iyan,” he said.
“Ang trabaho po nila is to secure yung kanilang Vice President,” Ortega added. He said the documents presented so far did not show that the officers had authority to use or distribute the money.

Maj. Gen. Adonis Bajao was initially among three military officials identified for testimony, but the prosecution later dropped him after the court had difficulty serving a subpoena. Boransing and Panopio remain scheduled. /cb

articles.title: Warnings over squishy toy hazards expand globally
articles.summary: Squishy toys have triggered recalls, seizures and burn warnings abroad. Health Canada has received 36 reports involving squishy dumpling toys, including injuries, but says it has not confirmed a…

image.caption: Squishy bun toy containing water beads. (U.S. Consumer Product Safety Commission)

blocks.text: Health

Squishy toys have triggered recalls, seizures and burn warnings abroad. Health Canada has received 36 reports involving squishy dumpling toys, including injuries, but says it has not confirmed a specific health or safety risk.
Regulators have flagged benzene in some products, burn risks from counterfeits and toys bursting in heat

Some trendy squishy toys have prompted burn warnings and enforcement action in several countries, while Canadian regulators say they've received dozens of reports but have not confirmed a specific health or safety risk.

The soft, palm-sized toys come in a variety of shapes, including cubes and spheres, as well as food shapes such as dumplings and sticks of butter. Their squishy texture is a defining feature of toys marketed for sensory play and sold through online marketplaces, discount stores and other retailers.
Regulators raise concerns abroad
This week, Cornwall Trading Standards in southwest England, warned that some squishy toys they tested failed U.K. safety standards.

Separately, Hull City Council in northeast England said it seized and destroyed toys from local retailers after testing found high levels of benzene, a carcinogen. Hull officials said high levels of exposure can cause irritation of the eyes, nose and throat, skin irritation and, if ingested, a burning sensation.
The local actions in England followed a recall by the U.K.'s Office for Product Safety and Standards of Squeezy Dumplings in June.
Some squishy toys are not safe, health officials warn

Earlier this month, the U.S. Consumer Product Safety Commission reiterated a warning about serious burn hazards associated with fake and counterfeit squishy toys that do not comply with U.S. safety requirements.
Shipments of what the agency called "violative squishy toys" have also been seized at U.S. ports.
In Australia, Schyling, the manufacturer of NeeDoh toys, has reportedly asked the Australian Border Force to intercept counterfeit versions of its products.
Health Canada has received 36 reports
From April 23 to Aug. 24, Health Canada said it received 36 reports involving squishy dumpling toys.

"There were 30 reports of odours, four reports about the sale of these products but with no mention of odour or injury, and two reports of the product exploding, with 6 of these reports mentioning an injury (e.g., headache, skin rash, difficulty breathing)," Health Canada said in a statement to CBC News. "These reports include both children and adults."
Health Canada said it has not identified any failures to comply with health or safety regulations and has not confirmed that the toys pose a specific health or safety risk.
Separately, Amazon Canada said in a statement that it proactively removed some squishy dumpling toys following reported safety concerns.
What is actually inside the toys?

Toy manufacturers are not obligated to disclose the ingredients and may not always know exactly what is in their products, said Miriam Diamond, a professor and environmental chemist at the University of Toronto who studies microplastics and chemicals in consumer products.

items: Do kids still want toys? Toy stores are struggling, but don't just blame screens
CBC's What on Earth | Is plastic-free plastic even possible?

blocks.text: "There could be chemicals there that are fairly benign, but there could also be chemicals that are of concern. I don't know, and that's actually concerning in and of itself," Diamond said, calling on manufacturers and importers to be vigilant.
Do squishies actually work? The history of sensory toys
The product safety group Consumer Reports said concerns are not necessarily limited to counterfeit or off-brand products.

"We kind of feel that it's not just about the counterfeit," said Ashita Kapoor, director of product safety and personal care at Consumer Reports. "We're actually seeing incidents of products that are happening that are purchased directly from retail."
Tips for parents
For now, the U.S. Product Safety Commission advises families to:

items: Keep affected toys away from heat, including hot cars and prolonged sunlight, and never intentionally heat them.
Inspect toys regularly for leaks.
Use caution when cleaning up after a toy bursts to avoid direct skin contact.

blocks.text: Diamond also suggests families declutter and stick with a few simple toys.
Families should also follow recommended age limits.
NeeDoh and Squishy Dumpling did not respond to requests for comment.
With files from CBC's Tahlia Sarv

blocks.text: BAGUIO CITY, Philippines — A 64-year-old pedestrian was killed while four vehicles were damaged in a road crash at the junction of Magsaysay Avenue and Hilltop Street at around 4 p.m. on Friday, Aug. 28, the Baguio City Police Office (BCPO) said.

BCPO chief Col. Ruel Tagel said the victim was struck by an Isuzu closed van driven by a 48-year-old man after the vehicle allegedly experienced mechanical trouble while traveling downhill along Hilltop Street toward Magsaysay Avenue.
The van then collided with a Toyota Hilux pickup driven by a 28-year-old businessman and a Toyota Innova driven by a 21-year-old student, police said.
The impact caused the Innova to swerve toward the outer lane, where it hit another Toyota Innova taxi driven by a 44-year-old man.

Responding Bureau of Fire Protection personnel provided initial medical assistance to the pedestrian. He was later declared dead by Baguio City Emergency Medical Service head and medical officer Dandeo Halog.
The four vehicles sustained damage of undetermined value.
Tagel said an investigation is underway to determine the exact circumstances of the crash and the possible liability of those involved. —MAUREEN MATAYEW/CONTRIBUTOR

articles.title: Number of Australians missing in Nepal’s deadly floods rises again, as Albanese deploys more personnel
articles.summary: There are now 41 Australians missing, and four rapid response team members are expected to arrive in Kathmandu
articles.byline: Stephanie Convery and Cait Kelly in Kathmandu

blocks.text: The number of Australians who were reported missing in the catastrophic Nepal flooding disaster has risen to 41, as one family celebrates after an unaccounted-for woman made contact with them yesterday.
It means three additional Australians were confirmed missing overnight – up from 38 who remained unaccounted for on Friday evening.

The Australian government’s Department of Foreign Affairs has been urgently working with local authorities to contact Australian woman Cara Severino, 25, who became the first Australian reported missing who has been confirmed safe.

Severino contacted her parents, Debbie and Frank Severino, on Friday morning, informing them she was hiking away from the disaster zone to Kathmandu with a group of Nepali hikers – a trek of more than 110km.

The Red Cross has said about 600 people are dead and as many as 93,000 people may have been affected by Wednesday’s flash floods on the Nepal-Tibet border, with a huge rescue operation that is being hampered by fears of new flooding.
Dfat has received more than 450 calls in relation to the disaster.

blocks.caption: Some of Australia’s missing in Nepal as of Friday, 28 August. Clockwise from left: Karan Bhardwaj, Chitra Venkatraman, Venkatraman Balakrishnan, Sumi Adhikari and family: Shylaja Muralitharan, Aarush Muralitharan, Ashwin Muralitharan & Chandrasekaran Muralitharan. Composite: Supplied by the families

blocks.text: Nepal’s disaster management agency says there are 1,924 people unaccounted for – 517 of those people are foreign tourists.
About 7:30pm on Friday evening, the authority said 121 foreigners had been rescued – none of them were Australians.
View from Kathmandu hospital
Outside the hospital in Kathmandu yesterday, there were scenes of anxiety as families put up posters of loved ones, and authorities hung pictures of the dead that need to be identified.
One woman said her cousin was on his way back from Australia because his brother had gone missing.
Like many others, she was putting pictures of him up, in case he was brought back to the hospital.

Australian charities are starting to pump in aid, with the Emergency Action Alliance – a peak body representing major Australian charities – raising funds to build emergency shelters, get food and safe drinking water, hygiene supplies and medical care to communities.

But conditions on the ground are difficult and unpredictable owing to the scale of the damage and the heavy monsoon. Rescue operations in Nepal and China resumed as of Saturday morning after being suspended due to the risk of further flooding.

blocks.caption: An aerial view shows the aftermath of massive flooding along the Bhotekoshi River, which affected low-lying areas and settlements near the riverbanks in Nuwakot, Nepal.  Photograph: Ap Tolang/Nexpher/ZUMA Press Wire/Shutterstock
The flooding caused widespread damage to homes, roads, bridge, hydropower station and other infrastructure in the area.  Photograph: Ap Tolang/Nexpher/ZUMA Press Wire/Shutterstock

blocks.text: Four Dfat crisis response team officers are expected to arrive in Kathmandu later on Saturday to support consular efforts on the ground.
Four rapid response team members are also expected to arrive in Kathmandu – humanitarian response specialists with expertise in communications, logistics and planning.
These extra deployments add to about 20 personnel Australian already has on the ground with the Australian embassy in Kathmandu.

On Friday night, the foreign affairs minister, Penny Wong, spoke with the Nepali foreign minister, Shisir Khanal, to affirm that Australia would provide further humanitarian assistance, including to aid rescue and recovery efforts, where required.

Australia has pledged $5m in aid and support for the disaster, with $2m going to the World Food Programme to provide emergency food and water provisions, and the remaining to the Emergency Action Alliance.

Australia’s assistant minister for foreign affairs and trade, Matt Thistlethwaite, said on Saturday morning that the aid was being provided on request of the Nepalese authorities. Speaking to ABC News Breakfast, Thistlethwaite said Australian officials in Beijing were also working with the Chinese Government, but that China had not so far requested support.
“We’re doing our best to support both the Nepalese and Tibetan diasporas here in Australia,” Thistlethwaite said.

“Yesterday I held two online forums, one with the Nepalese community one with the Tibetan community to outline the latest situation, to advise of the support that Australia is providing, the $5m in humanitarian aid, and the best way for us to keep in contact with them. We’re providing them with the latest information through our officials.

“I also attended a vigil last night with the Nepalese community in Strathfield and obviously there was quite a bit of despair and anxiety in that community, but we’re doing our best to support the Tibetan and Nepalese communities here in Australia.”

articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — The Office of the Ombudsman on Friday said they are still gathering evidence against former Executive Secretary Lucas Bersamin and two other officials tagged by a state witness…

blocks.caption: Assistant Ombudsman Mico Clavano —Photo from Mico Clavano/Facebook

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — The Office of the Ombudsman on Friday said they are still gathering evidence against former Executive Secretary Lucas Bersamin and two other officials tagged by a state witness in the alleged kickback scheme.

Assistant Ombudsman Mico Clavano said their action against Bersamin, his grandnephew, former Undersecretary Adrian Bersamin of the Presidential Legislative Liaison Office, and former Education Undersecretary Trygve Olaivar is still under fact-finding.

“They are included in the second case, which the Ombudsman already described as a grand conspiracy to defraud the 2025 budget,” Clavano said in a press conference when asked about the update on the cases of Bersamins and Olaivar.

“That case is still in fact-finding, and we are sifting through the facts and the documents that were given to us,” he said, referring to those turned over by the Independent Commission for Infrastructure and Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH).
Former DPWH Undersecretary Roberto Bernardo tagged the three individuals in the kickback scheme during a Senate blue ribbon committee hearing last year.
Bernardo claimed he met with Education Undersecretary Trygve Olaivar in 2024 to discuss unprogrammed appropriations supposedly intended for the Office of the Executive Secretary.
The former DPWH Undersecretary further alleged that Olaivar requested a 15-percent cut from the P2.85-billion infrastructure projects for Bersamin’s office. Bersamin denied this allegation.
Clavano said they are “listening to him because he is a state witness and he has been cooperating with us.
“We do find him credible, and his statements are being used as leads to point us in the right direction,” he said, while noting that his statements should be corroborated by other evidence.

Meanwhile, the younger Bersamin was identified by resigned Ako Bicol party-list Rep. articles.title: Search for 3 missing Aetas in Zambales suspended due to weather
articles.summary: SAN ANTONIO, ZAMBALES, Philippines — Search and rescue operations for three Aetas still missing after the boat they were riding in capsized in Mapanuepe Lake in San Marcelino town were suspended…

blocks.caption: Search and rescue operations conducted in Mapanuepe Lake, San Marcelino, Zambales, on Friday, for three Aetas still missing after their boat capsized —Photo courtesy of PCG

blocks.text: SAN ANTONIO, ZAMBALES, Philippines — Search and rescue operations for three Aetas still missing after the boat they were riding in capsized in Mapanuepe Lake in San Marcelino town were suspended Friday (Aug. 28) due to worsening weather conditions.
The search was halted several times throughout the day as responders faced unfavorable weather, briefly resuming when conditions improved before being suspended again in the afternoon.

On Thursday (Aug. 27), a boat carrying 13 Aeta community members capsized near the Sunken Church in Barangay Buhawen. Four of them survived, six died and three – a pregnant woman and two children still missing.

Based on reports from the Philippine Coast Guard, they first reached the incident area at 5:01 a.m. and conducted preparations, an initial assessment and a seaborne patrol before temporarily suspending the operation due to adverse weather conditions.
By 8:40 a.m., responding agencies had convened under the Incident Command System (ICS) to coordinate the search and assign operational tasks.
A reported cadaver sighting at Mapanuepe Campsite Phase 2 was also checked at 11:10 a.m., but responders found no body.
The search resumed at 12:15 p.m. after weather conditions improved, with four floating assets deployed to scour the identified search area and surrounding waters.
After an operational debriefing at 3:30 p.m., the search was suspended again at 4:10 p.m. due to inclement weather and expected to resume on Saturday (Aug. 29). /cb

articles.title: Zero-fee GCash remittances open for OFWs in Bahrain
articles.summary: Digital money transfer provider Taptap Send and GCash, the Philippines’ largest mobile wallet operator, have expanded their cross-border remittance network to Bahrain, targeting the growing market of…

blocks.text: Digital money transfer provider Taptap Send and GCash, the Philippines’ largest mobile wallet operator, have expanded their cross-border remittance network to Bahrain, targeting the growing market of overseas Filipino workers (OFWs) seeking lower transfer costs.
In a statement, GCash said the partnership allows Filipinos in the Middle Eastern nation to send funds directly into recipient GCash accounts in the Philippines.
Under a temporary promotional agreement, the companies are offering zero transfer fees on transactions originating from Bahrain, though standard foreign exchange conversion margins still apply.

Beyond Bahrain, the companies plan to extend the integrated service to major migrant worker destinations including the United States, Canada, the United Kingdom, the United Arab Emirates, Australia, and 27 European nations.

“Our partnership with GCash allows us to make it even easier for overseas Filipinos to send money home through a trusted digital platform,” said Faye Sta. Ana-Corpuz, head of Philippines growth and Southeast Asia expansion at Taptap Send.
She added that competitive foreign exchange rates and zero transaction fees across supported corridors aim to help workers maximize their transfers home.

The company also seeks to divert money flows away from informal, unaccredited remittance channels toward licensed electronic networks, which offer regulators and users clearer transaction logs and security.

“By working with trusted international partners like Taptap Send, we are expanding access to safe, convenient, and reliable ways for Filipinos abroad to send money home while strengthening their connection to the Philippines,” said Carlos Bauza, vice president for international payments at GCash International.

To execute a transfer, senders download the Taptap Send application, select the Philippines as the receiving destination, choose GCash as the settlement method, and input the recipient's mobile phone number registered under either Philippine country code +63 or Bahrain country code +973. Once verified, the digital funds clear instantly into the recipient's GCash wallet balance.

articles.title: BIR pushes electronic invoicing rollout as Dec. 31 deadline nears
articles.summary: The Bureau of Internal Revenue (BIR) is moving forward with its digital transformation initiative designed to modernize the country’s tax administration, consulting private-sector representatives to…

blocks.text: Bureau of Internal Revenue (BIR) Commissioner Charlito Martin R. Mendoza (left) speaks alongside BIR Deputy Commissioner Vener S. Baquiran during a consultation on proposed electronic invoicing guidelines at the BIR National Office in Quezon City.

The Bureau of Internal Revenue (BIR) is moving forward with its digital transformation initiative designed to modernize the country’s tax administration, consulting private-sector representatives to refine upcoming electronic invoicing guidelines.

Led by BIR Commissioner Charlito Martin R. Mendoza, the tax authority hosted a public consultation at its National Office with the BIR Partnership with the Multisectoral Group, seeking technical feedback from the business community as implementation approaches.
The discussions centered on aligning proposed administrative rules with practical corporate workflows across various industries.
“Electronic invoicing is part of the legacy work we are building at the BIR,” Mendoza said during the forum.
“We have to get the Electronic Invoicing System project off the ground, learn from actual implementation, and improve as we go. Your input will help us get this right,” he added.
The draft Revenue Memorandum Circular operationalizes electronic invoicing requirements under Section 237 of the Tax Code and relevant regulations.

Taxpayers designated under the initial phase must transition to electronic invoicing by Dec. 31, 2026. Submissions under subsequent phased rollouts will be governed by future administrative issuances.

Under the proposed framework, covered corporate entities may build in-house systems, procure commercially available software, or contract third-party solution providers to manage invoice issuance and transmission.
The transition aims to move away from traditional paper-based auditing, aiming to reduce tax leakage, enhance revenue visibility, and streamline data collection.
Representatives from key commercial sectors—including accounting, tax consultancy, finance, technology, petroleum, foreign chambers, and export industries—participated in the sessions.
The bureau noted that suggestions gathered during the consultation will inform the final draft of the guidelines ahead of formal publication.

“Electronic invoicing is an important part of modernizing tax administration,” Mendoza said. “We want to move this reform forward in a way that works for taxpayers and businesses and gives them greater confidence in the systems they rely on.”
The bureau will finalize the circular in the coming weeks as it prepares infrastructure and stakeholder support for the compliance deadline.

articles.title: Ottawa couple's 'Lake Ontario' hats selling like hotcakes after Trump's executive order
articles.summary: Before the ink had even dried on U.S. President Donald Trump's executive order to rename Lake Ontario, a Canadian company was already selling hats with the Great Lake's true name emblazoned on it.

image.caption: Canadian company Jackpine began selling Lake Ontario hats just hours after U.S. President Donald Trump signed an executive order to rename the Great Lake on U.S. maps. (jackpine.co)

blocks.text: As It Happens
Before the ink had even dried on U.S. President Donald Trump's executive order to rename Lake Ontario, a Canadian company was already selling hats with the Great Lake's true name emblazoned on it.
Canadian company Jackpine also behind the viral 'Canada's Not For Sale' hats
LISTEN | Interview with Ottawa apparel company owner Liam Mooney:
As It Happens6:01Ottawa company's 'Lake Ontario' hats selling like hotcakes in wake of Trump executive order
The baseball caps from Ottawa company Jackpine went up for sale online just hours after Trump signed the order to call the body of water that borders Canada and New York "Lake America."
Jackpine founder Liam Mooney says he came up with the idea for the design the night before.
"It was just clear that he was going to do this to us, and so we jumped on it," Mooney told As It Happens guest host Paul Hunter. "The timing was certainly fortuitous."

Jackpine, which Mooney owns with his wife Emma Cochrane, is also responsible for the "Canada Is Not For Sale" hats that became a sensation last year after Ontario Premier Doug Ford started sporting one during public appearances.
"I feel like, you know, in a certain sense, like an obligation, like I'm a chief propagandist for Canada," Mooney said.

"I'm just sort of doing whatever I can to activate our made-in-Canada supply chains so that if there is demand from this, that we can onshore that manufacturing and that we use the project itself to activate the industrial base of our country."
Trump's executive order, which changes the Great Lake's name on U.S. maps, comes after trade negotiations broke down between Canada and the U.S. last weekend.
The Trump administration has slapped 50 per cent tariffs on a wide array of Canadian goods, and Canada has responded in kind.
Canadians have flatly rejected the executive order.

Prime Minister Mark Carney wrote on social media that the name Ontario comes from the Wendat word Ontari’io," which means “'the lake is beautiful, the lake is big," and noted it predates "both the Confederation of Canada and the Declaration of Independence of the United States of America."
Wendat Nation Grand Chief Pierre Picard also issued a statement accusing Trump of trying to "eradicate" the nation's history.
Trump orders Lake Ontario be renamed 'Lake America'
U.S. political commentator Charlie Sykes told CBC Radio's Day 6 the move shows how unserious Trump is as a leader.

"He's trying to portray himself as this, you know, great world-bestriding leader, comparing himself to the Caesars and the Napoleons and the Attila the Huns of history. But what is he doing? He's sitting around on social media, putting out a slop about changing the names of lakes," Syles said.
"A clown with a flamethrower still has a flamethrower, but he's still a clown too."
Cashing in on patriotism?
Mooney says the minute Jackpine posted the hat online, the orders started flooding in.
"It's been a really awesome day, a really tremendous response," he said. "Canadians, I think, are looking for opportunities right now to channel their patriotism."
But the customer base, he says, extends beyond Canada's borders.
"We're getting order in Paris, Tokyo, London, Berlin," he said. "People around the world are standing in solidarity with Canada."

items: 'Lake America'? Trump's 'utterly ridiculous' renaming met with laughter in Kingston
Despite Trump's renaming of Lake Ontario, Great Lakes endure as symbol of U.S.-Canada collaboration

blocks.text: His isn't the only Canadian company that's found a way to cash in on the trade war that's expected to wreak havoc on many businesses and industries.
In 2025, "Elbows Up" apparel was flying off the shelves of Canadian companies, including Timeless Memories in Yarmouth, N.S., and Toronto's Shop Love Collective.
The hockey phrase, coined by legendary player Gordie Howe, became a national rallying cry last spring when Trump was making repeated jokes and threats about annexing Canada as a 51st state.
This Windsor, Ont., woman is making hundreds of 'Elbows Up' pins
Asked whether selling the Lake Ontario hats could be seen as a cynical ploy to make a buck off a bad situation, Mooney maintained he's motivated by patriotism, not profits.

"When people are looking for a way to express how they feel, to take a lot of complex ideas and put it somewhere really simple, there are ways to do that. And it just so happens that we've been fortunate enough to be a part of some moments where we've actually accomplished that," he said.
"And thankfully, it's been to Canada's benefit. We've invested millions into the Canadian textile industry, into Canadian workers."
Interview with Liam Mooney produced by Chris Harbord

articles.title: Footage of Tibet floods isn't being shown in China - and we know little about victims there
articles.summary: Some of the most dramatic footage from the deadly flash flooding is hidden from public view in China.

blocks.text: The dramatic footage was almost impossible to miss. A torrent of water tearing through Gyirong Port, one of the main border crossings between Nepal and Tibet, sweeping away all in its path as hundreds of people fled for their lives.
The scenes, captured by CCTV cameras, quickly spread on social media and onto screens around the world.
Except here, in China.
Only a single still-frame shot has been broadcast so far by the country's state-run flagship news bulletin.

It has also been difficult to find the video on China's heavily censored internet. It is just as hard to even find posts describing the flash flooding that has claimed hundreds of lives, with just as many still unaccounted for since Wednesday.

Beijing has launched a massive rescue operation involving hundreds of emergency workers, which is continuing, and President Xi Jinping chaired an emergency meeting with officials to co-ordinate efforts.
But when you compare the country's internet content to what much of the world has been seeing online these past few days, China's firewall becomes more visible than ever.
Tibet, which Beijing annexed in the 1950s, had long resisted rule by the Chinese Communist Party.

China has quashed protests over the years, sometimes violently, and has been accused of grave rights violations in the Buddhist region. It has labelled the exiled spiritual leader, the Dalai Lama, a separatist.
That history means the very name Tibet draws China's censors. Beijing's sensitivities are especially apparent at times likes this.

There have been daily updates on the missing and the dead, and Beijing has also been posting updates on the rescue operations, as well as the dangers posed by a barrier lake that has been at risk of overflowing.
But there is little detail beyond that. There are no accounts from survivors in Tibet, and almost no user-generated footage showing the deadly moments or their aftermath.
We are yet to hear from anxious families of those missing. Trying to contact people there is near-impossible during regular times.
As a journalist who has covered North Korea, it has often been easier for me to contact interviewees in Pyongyang than it is in the Tibetan capital, Lhasa.

On Thursday night, as global headlines led on the devastation in a Himalayan valley, China's state broadcaster opened its main bulletin with the launch of Xi's new book, a selection of his "most important and fundamental works".

Foreign journalists cannot travel to Tibet without government permission. We have just a few hours to get as much information as we can on huge stories like this before videos are scrubbed and voices stifled.
Instead, we have to rely on state media, which has so far focused on incredibly dramatic rescue efforts.

Specialist search teams scaling mountains and cliff faces, or crossing raging rivers to try to get to the worst-affected areas. We don't yet know what happened afterwards, or who they were able to save.
This is not to say that Beijing is unconcerned. Rather, they are very concerned.
China's Premier Li Qiang was quickly despatched to the region, where he was seen inspecting debris removal - a rare visit by the country's second-most important leader so soon after a major disaster.
The reason for what the world might see as a muted response is to preserve the one thing Xi covets for his country: stability.
The Communist Party will fear that such a disaster could fuel discontent, either with the response or the lack of foresight to prevent it.
It may also fear the impact of a tragedy like this and its potential to be a rallying factor, especially in a community where faith has long played a central role.

Although the region has not seen protests in a long time, Tibetan groups abroad have expressed concern over increasing Chinese control, such as new education laws that they say aim to weaken the role of monasteries and the Buddhist faith.
Just hours after the disaster struck, the Communist Party machine tried to rally its grassroots to stem any signs of discontent of its handling of the landslide.
A notice came from the local party office urging members to step up and help in disaster relief efforts in their area and provide emotional guidance or psychological support to affected residents.

The key line instructs them to "make every effort to maintain social order and ensure stability and public confidence in the disaster areas". Those who perform well would be rewarded - and those who do badly "would be held accountable".

It is a warning that will not be taken lightly. Tibetans in the region can be detained or arrested for speaking to journalists or posting anything online that is seen as contrary to the government narrative, according to rights activists.
That is making it difficult for Tibetans outside the region to find out what has happened to their relatives.

The International Campaign for Tibet, while praising the work of first responders in the area, said Beijing had been removing videos and other first-hand information from social media. It called on Chinese authorities to "disclose complete and verifiable information about the damage and casualties".

To try to understand what life is like for Tibetans, the BBC travelled to a town that sits on the edge of the Himalayan plateau last year - just outside what China calls the Tibetan Autonomous region.
There, we spoke to monks at the Kirti monastery in Aba, or Ngaba in Tibetan, which was once at the heart of its resistance to Beijing. "We Tibetans are denied basic human rights," one monk told us.

They said they lived under constant surveillance and claimed the Chinese government oppressed and persecuted Tibetans. The conversations were brief because we could not be seen speaking to anyone for long.
Beijing denies it is violating Tibetans' rights, and points to the heavy investments it has made in the region to boost tourism and integrate it with the rest of the country.
Nevertheless, people in China will not know very much about what is happening in Tibet right now.
