articles.title: Postpartum psychosis is terrifying but treatable, this survivor says. The challenge is finding support
articles.summary: A decade ago, Meghan Cliffel believed she was being watched by members of a cult who were out to kill her and her young daughters. In fact, she was experiencing postpartum psychosis, the condition at…

image.caption: Meghan Cliffel is pregnant here with her second daughter. In December 2015, she experienced postpartum psychosis, and she says she wants people to know that it's treatable. (Submitted by Meghan Cliffel)

blocks.text: WARNING: This article contains details about violence against children and suicide.
When Meghan Cliffel stepped onto the subway in New York City after work and caught the eyes of her fellow passengers, she felt as though something had gone gravely wrong.

While those around her scrolled on their phones or listened to music, the mother-of-two believed they were surveilling her. She switched trains, trying to throw off the supposed pursuers and then continued on to a gathering of old friends.

But the unease persisted; eventually, she ran across the city to get home, thinking someone might be about to harm her family when a friend innocuously asked who was watching her daughters, then two and eight months old.

"My brain is knitting things together into this kind of complex reality where I believe there's some kind of cultish scheme running the city," she said. "I am in the centre of it in some way and they're out to get me and my kids."

In fact, she had postpartum psychosis, a rare condition that affects about one to two mothers per 1,000 births and is currently at the heart of Lindsay Clancy's defence in her first-degree murder trial in Massachusetts, where she is accused of killing her three children.
LISTEN | What postpartum psychosis feel like:
The Current24:41Lindsay Clancy trial shines light postpartum mental health

The disorder is considered a psychiatric emergency and requires immediate treatment, said Nicholas Leyland, president of the Society of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists of Canada (SOGC) who is based in Ontario. Symptoms include delusions, visual or auditory hallucinations, distorted thinking, paranoia, mania or depression, insomnia and confusion.
But when Cliffel experienced her first delusions on Dec. 4, 2015, she said neither she nor her husband had heard of the disorder.
'Excruciating to watch'

Now, a decade later, she is healthy, a mother of three and a writer and maternal mental health advocate. And she finds it "excruciating to watch" the Clancy proceedings, she said, because she can envision her own experience ending similarly had her husband left her alone with the children — and because postpartum psychosis is temporary and treatable.
One of the biggest challenges, however, as she and Clancy found, can be getting a diagnosis.

Jurors are now deliberating whether the 36-year-old former labour and delivery nurse should be held criminally responsible for killing her children, Cora, 5; Dawson, 3; and eight-month-old Callan in 2023 while her then-husband was out on an errand.

She is accused of strangling the children with exercise bands in the basement of her Boston-area home before leaping out a second-storey window after cutting her neck in an attempt to take her own life. She is now paralyzed and uses a wheelchair.
Her defence team has argued that Clancy cannot be held criminally responsible, saying her medical condition created a distorted sense of reality.

Her lawyers described Clancy as doing all she could to get help for her deteriorating mental health — both from family and through numerous health-care providers, who, collectively, prescribed her 13 different medications. She called a suicide hotline, went to the emergency room and checked herself into a psychiatric facility. She had been denied an outpatient spot at a postpartum mental health program.
These attempts, women's health advocates and Clancy's supporters say, underscore the systemic failures of the health-care system for women and, by extension, their children.
Missing from the DSM-5
In custody, Clancy got her diagnosis: bipolar disorder and postpartum psychosis.
"It feels a little bit like a different version of my life," Cliffel said. "And the second reason it feels excruciating is because I know we can do so much better."

Now a postpartum mental health advocate based in Cleveland, Ohio, Cliffel said it is critical to update the DSM-5 — the handbook of psychiatric and mood disorders used across North America — to include postpartum psychosis as a standalone condition, not a subcategory of psychosis.
Doing so would create more awareness among doctors, psychologists and other maternal health specialists, she said, and likely increase the amount of investment and research into the condition.
And it might help others get an early diagnosis.

Cliffel spent 12 days at Bellevue Psychiatric hospital in New York City; her husband called emergency services the morning of Dec. 5, 2015, when she began punching him to try to get to their children and also threatening to jump from the roof.
"I wake up in a twin bed in the dark and I think I've been captured," she recalled. "I try and escape several times, because I think maybe my baby girls are still alive."

items: What is postpartum psychosis, the illness at the centre of Lindsay Clancy's murder trial?
Postpartum depression or anxiety reported by nearly a quarter of moms: StatsCan

blocks.text: Her condition improved with medication. After she was discharged, she spent six weeks in outpatient care but still didn't get a diagnosis.
Without answers about such a "ground-shifting experience," Cliffel said she had even more difficulty trusting whether her thoughts were real.
So she asked to see a psychiatrist who was also a mother.
"That got me into the chair of somebody who understood reproductive psychiatry," she said. "So it took, you know, about two months after I experienced it for somebody to label it."
Misdiagnoses

After nearly four decades of teaching health-care providers about maternal mental health, Karen Kleiman said she is still surprised by how many obstetricians consider sending patients to the emergency room for psychiatric evaluation instead of doing an assessment.
She blames some missed cases or misdiagnoses of postpartum psychosis on the businesslike evolution of medicine.

"The reality is in the medical community, they've got what? Three, four, seven minutes … to do a rapid assessment," said Kleiman, founder of The Postpartum Stress Center in Pennsylvania and author of Good Moms Have Scary Thoughts. "It's not part of their job description; it's beyond the scope of their practice. But at the same time, how long does it take to ask one or two good questions?"
Questions can help assess whether the patient is manic, whether the thoughts are manifesting in a more psychotic way — not worries about how to safely hold a baby.

"We cannot expect a woman who's very, very, very sick to tell us how bad she feels," said Kleiman, a registered social worker. "If there are psychotic symptoms going on, it's our burden to find that, to ask the right questions and to get her the help that she needs."
Risk assessment

It's why Elise Gwyn also does a risk assessment on new clients, whether it's before birth or afterward. The Ottawa-area psychotherapist specializes in perinatal mental health, which covers from pregnancy to a year postpartum, and encourages partners to join sessions so they can offer insight.

Risk factors for postpartum psychosis include a diagnosis or family history of bipolar disorder, while sensitivity to hormonal shifts can be a signal someone might experience a mood disorder after delivering, Gwyn said.

But it can be hard to parse the symptoms of postpartum psychosis, such as intrusive thoughts, from the healthy worries of a new mother or someone experiencing postpartum depression, anxiety or perinatal obsessive-compulsive disorder, Gwyn said, because the brain's "alarm system" is on high alert for risk to the baby.

That's why collateral information from partners can be critical, Gwyn said, since a psychotherapist, family doctor or obstetrician might only see a patient for a short period of time. Partners have the advantage of a shared home and history and can raise red flags a clinician might miss.
She, Kleiman and Cliffel all emphasized that while more education around diagnosis is important, the message that postpartum psychosis is temporary and treatable is just as critical.

With systemic change, Cliffel said — especially a standard of care that includes psychiatric screening and support — women with postpartum psychosis can not only recover but can be a healthy parent and even go on to have more children.
In November 2019, Cliffel gave birth for the third time: a baby boy.

She worked with a reproductive psychiatrist and therapist to create a plan for pregnancy and beyond. After delivery, she took lithium prophylactically for a year, and she wrote, practised mindfulness and stayed out of the labour force.
"We not only staved off recurrence but we experienced so much more joy the third time around," Cliffel said.
If you or someone you know is struggling, here's where to look for help:

items: Postpartum Support International Canada: Call 1-800-944-4773 or visit the website for support online.
Canada's Suicide Crisis Helpline: Call or text 988.
Provincial and territorial mental health support.
Kids Help Phone: 1-800-668-6868. Text 686868. Live chat counselling on the website.

articles.title: Health advocates push P80 vape tax to curb youth vaping
articles.summary: Public health advocates are urging Congress to impose a tax of at least P80 on vapor products, saying higher taxes are needed to discourage vaping among young Filipinos and prevent long-term health…

blocks.text: Published August 29, 2026 5:58am
Make this your preferred source to get more updates from this publisher on Google.

Public health advocates are urging Congress to impose a tax of at least P80 on vapor products, saying higher taxes are needed to discourage vaping among young Filipinos and prevent long-term health costs.

The Healthy Philippines Alliance (HPA), with HealthJustice as its convener, said the proposed unified tax rate of P72.93 by 2027 for cigarettes, heated tobacco products (HTPs), and vapor products remains insufficient to curb access to vaping products.
The proposed rate was recommended by the Department of Finance (DOF) and the Department of Health (DOH).
HPA Lead Convener and former Health Secretary Dr. Jaime Galvez Tan said vaping products should not be considered harmless, warning of their potential impact on young people’s health.
“Vapes are far from harm-free,” Galvez Tan said, adding that the early development of chronic heart and lung conditions could eventually result in significant costs for the healthcare system.
HealthJustice also opposed proposals from some lawmakers to lower the vape tax to as little as P15 per milliliter.

HealthJustice Legal Adviser Atty. Benedict Nisperos called such proposals “reckless and unacceptable,” arguing that lower taxes could make nicotine-containing vape products more accessible to young people.
“We cannot allow lower tax rates that enable more addictive substances, like nicotine salt vapes, to proliferate in the market,” Nisperos said.
The group also raised concerns over what it described as regulatory gaps in the Philippines compared with other Southeast Asian countries.

Nisperos said eight of the 11 ASEAN countries have completely banned vapor products, while the Philippines continues to allow their sale under Republic Act 11900, or the Vaporized Nicotine and Non-Nicotine Products Regulation Act. —VBL, GMA News

items: Nepal’s disaster authority raised sharply the number of missing to 1,924 on Friday, two days after devastating floods that killed at least 579 in the country. The number of missing includes 517 foreigners, as well as 933 workers on hydropower projects on the rivers where a wall of water powered down on Wednesday morning, according to the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority. The AP is reporting a higher figure, with almost 2,500 are missing and nearly 600 people killed.

Authorities in Nepal and China issued warnings about the risk of a second wave of flooding. Chinese authorities said an artificial lake had formed after a mudslide hit the Tibet-Nepal border, which risked “sending flood waters downstream”, according to state media. Nepal’s disaster authority said a lake that had formed by debris blocking a river at the site was also rising and ‌at risk of bursting. Amid the mounting fears over a second wave of flooding, families are rushing to Nepal to search for the 33 British nationals who are still missing.

Rescuers were forced to suspend their search for survivors, while residents who had returned to Rasuwa were told to evacuate their homes, with many seen fleeing up the hillsides to escape a possible surge in the river.

The Red Cross has said at least 93,000 people may have been affected by the disaster, triggering a huge rescue operation that is being hampered by fears of new flooding. The International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies (IFRC), the world’s largest humanitarian network, said it feared the death toll would continue to rise as some of the hardest-hit areas remained inaccessible after roads and bridges were destroyed by the torrents.

The European Union has promised €2m ($2.3m) in aid for Nepal. European Commission chief Ursula von der Leyen wrote on X that the “immediate humanitarian aid” would help “deliver life-saving assistance to families and communities hit hardest.”

Nepal has said it does not yet need foreign assistance as the search and rescue operation – complicated by the destruction of bridges and roads across the mountainous region – continues. “The offer for help is natural,” Lok Bahadur Chhetri, a spokesperson for Nepal’s foreign ministry, said on Friday. “Our security agencies ‌are doing the search and rescue operation. For now we don’t require such help.”

Rescue teams have reported finding bodies hundreds of miles downstream from the disaster zone in the Chitwan district of Nepal, near the Tibetan border. Dozens of injured people were transported to Kathmandu for advanced medical care and more than 100 people were rescued by Nepali army personnel in helicopters.

blocks.text: The number of missing individuals in the deadly flash flood has risen past 2,400, according to a count by AFP.
Nepal’s disaster authority added 933 hydropower workers to a missing persons list already including trekkers and pilgrims to Tibet’s sacred Mount Kailash, AFP reported.
The news agency also reported that emergency teams have recovered 586 bodies so far – with some of the dead swept downstream as far away as India.
Our most recent reporting indicates that 1,924 individuals are missing and at least 579 were killed, as of Friday, two days after the devastating floods.
Chinese control of information hampers assessment of Tibet flood damage

blocks.caption: Amy Hawkins

blocks.text: Amy Hawkins

As the scale of the devastation caused by the flash floods in Nepal and Tibet unfolds, the picture is emerging far more quickly in Nepal than in China, where strict controls on the flow of information from one of its most sensitive regions are hampering the public’s understanding of events.

The floods devastated villages along the Himalayan border region that straddles Nepal and the Chinese region of Tibet. On Friday, the official death toll in Nepal rose to 538 people, while in China it was just five, despite the fact that the villages around the Gyirong border crossing are home to several thousand people.

“Everything about Tibet is seen through the national security prism. And therefore nobody is going to say anything or report anything that has not been cleared from the very top,” said Steve Tsang, the director of the China Institute at Soas University of London.
For anyone on the ground, “you can’t report a higher figure of deaths, even if you have seen more bodies yourself, until the official statement says that the figure has gone up”.

Tibet, brought under Chinese control in the 1950s, is the most sensitive and tightly controlled region in the country. Sporadic protests, including self-immolations, by Tibetans calling for more autonomy and religious freedom have been cracked down on by the authorities.

International journalists cannot visit Tibet apart from on tightly choreographed government tours. Many Tibetans are not allowed passports and have very limited contact with the outside world. Tibetans can be punished for speaking to journalists. Human rights groups have for years criticised Beijing’s policies on Tibetan language and culture, which activists say are under attack.
As the Chinese government’s tight controls on information limit international coverage of its relief efforts, it continues to stress that the disaster is a national priority.

China’s leader, Xi Jinping, chaired a meeting on Friday to direct rescue work, according to state media, in which he called on the authorities to “make every effort to search for missing people from China and abroad”.

He also dispatched his number two, premier Li Qiang, to visit the affected area. According to the state-run Xinhua news agency, Li “emphasised that General Secretary Xi Jinping is deeply concerned about the people in the disaster-stricken areas”.
'Now I have nothing left to live for,' survivors grieve relatives and homes swept away in Nepal flooding
Hannah Ellis-Petersen and Gaurav Pokharel in Bidur, Nepal.

Sangke Dolma Tamang, 61, had been cheerily cooking snacks in her village of Mailung in the Rasuwa district when the floods came without warning. The whole family ran uphill for safety, but as she grabbed for her husband, he slipped from her grip and was washed into the dark, fast-moving waters.

“Others tried to pull him to safety, but the flood swept him away,” she said, tears rolling down her weathered cheeks. There was, she said, nothing left of her village now. She had spent a night sheltering on higher ground, until an army helicopter arrived and brought to her safety at the barracks. Her son too was missing since the disaster, and she waited anxiously for any news.
“Now I have nothing left to live for,” said Tamang. “The whole house is gone. We couldn’t salvage anything.”

blocks.caption: Sangke Dolma Tamang (in red), 61, grieves her family and home in the aftermath of the deadly flooding in Nepal. Photograph: Ahmer Khan/The Guardian

blocks.text: As a melting glacier high up in the Himalayas between Tibet and Nepal splintered and crashed into the valley below, it set off a deadly cascade of water, mud and debris down the Bhote Koshi River. The Nepali village homes that lined the riverbank and clung to the mountainside stood little chance.

Two days after the disaster, at least 579 people have been confirmed dead and more than 1,900 are still missing, the numbers rising by the day. Many in Nepal fear that the true scale of the disaster has yet to emerge, as the worst-hit areas in districts such as Rusawa are only accessible by helicopter. The situation remains even more opaque in Tibet, which is under tight Chinese media control. Though it was at the centre of the disaster, Chinese authorities insist only five people there have died.

In the army barracks in the town of Bidur, where Nepal’s rescue efforts were being coordinated, helicopters carrying those rescued from flooded areas continued to arrive every few minutes, while others carrying vital supplies of food and clean water flew out and high up into the mountains.

blocks.caption: Flood victims evacuate to Nepal army camp - loop

blocks.text: On Friday morning, ground rescue efforts were halted over fears that the river levels were rising once again. But the Nepali army spokesperson, Brig Gen Raja Ram Basnet, said the helicopter rescues would continue for as long as people were missing. He accepted that the death toll was hard to calculate. “Right now, our focus is mostly on finding the living,” he said.

Among those recently brought to safety was 60-year-old Murali Maiya Tamang, who had been in Rusawa and was found hanging in a tree. As the flash floods came down the valley, she had watched as her house was washed clean away. She convulsed with tears as she waited desperately for news of her son, who was in their village when the floods struck and has been missing since.
“My husband had already died in Nepal’s 2015 earthquake,” she said. “Now this flood has taken away the only son I had left. I am all alone now. What is the point of living now?”

Here are some images coming through on the news wires of residents salvaging their belongings after the deadly flash flooding in Nepal.

A woman carries a bag and suitcase of her belongings after her house was heavily covered in mud.  Photograph: Manan Vatsyayana/AFP/Getty Images
Residents salvage belongings from their destroyed home.  Photograph: Ezra Acayan/Getty Images

blocks.text: Footage shows glacier collapse that led to deadly flooding in Nepal – video

This drone video shared with the Guardian shows the moment of glacier collapse that led to the devastating flash flooding in Nepal. The numbers of people missing, killed or injured are feared to continue to rise as rescue efforts are under way.
The UK has deployed a rapid response team of specially trained volunteers to Nepal to help with the disaster there.
The foreign secretary Ed Miliband said: “The scenes from Nepal are devastating, and our thoughts remain with everyone affected.

“The safety and welfare of British nationals is our top priority. That is why we are deploying a Rapid Deployment Team to Nepal to provide additional support on the ground for British nationals and their families at what is an incredibly difficult time.
“Our staff are working closely with the Nepali authorities, emergency responders and our embassy in Kathmandu to ensure those affected can access the assistance and information they need.
“We will continue to do everything we can to support British nationals impacted by this tragedy.”
British nationals in Nepal who require consular assistance should contact the British Embassy in Kathmandu or call the FCDO on +44 (0)20 7008 5000.
Death toll in China rises to seven
The death toll has risen to seven and 554 remain missing after the mudslide at a border port in China’s Xizang region, according to local reports.
Zoyal Ghale, who ran ⁠into a forest and climbed trees to escape Nepal’s deadly floods, was reunited with his mother after she had begun to fear he and his brother had both perished in their school.

A day earlier, 8-year-old Ghale had been airlifted alone from the devastated northern district of ⁠Rasuwa with a broken leg and cuts on ⁠his face, while his mother, Matti Maya Tamang, 28, moved from one shelter and collection point to another looking for her two missing children.

“At the fourth place too, my children’s names were not on the list, and they were not there,” Tamang told Reuters. “I had come to accept that both my children ⁠were no more. All I could do was weep. I couldn’t hold myself together at all.“
Australians are searching for loved ones missing in floods along the Nepal-Tibet border as aid groups warn of a looming humanitarian disaster.
Several Australians with family in the affected region have flown to assist the search for survivors, combing towns impacted by debris and torrents of mud.
Among them is the husband of NSW mother-of-two Reshma Patel, who was due to touch down in Kathmandu on Friday.
Like the majority of the 38 Australians confirmed missing, Patel was making a pilgrimage with a tour group when the floods began.
Her last known location was an immigration office along the Nepal-Tibet border, which was captured on viral footage being inundated by floodwaters.
“She was inside the big building, which you can see in all the videos that had been hit hard by the floods at the border,” family friend Chin Valsan told AAP.
“After that, there is no contact whatsoever.”
‘Erased before their eyes’: desperate rescue efforts continue after Nepal-Tibet floods - podcast
Rescue efforts are continuing in Nepal and Tibet after flash floods that have killed hundreds and left many more missing.
But fears that a lake formed by the landslide could overflow and cause fresh flooding, along with difficulty accessing disaster-hit areas, are hindering rescue and recovery missions.
In today’s edition of The Latest podcast, Lucy Hough speaks with the Guardian’s south Asia correspondent Hannah Ellis-Petersen, who is in Nepal, about the situation on the ground.
Canada has announced CAN$5 million (£2.65m) in aid for the Nepal flood relief, the AFP news agency reported.

At least 93,000 ‘in great need’ after Nepal-Tibet flash floods, says Red Cross

blocks.caption: Hannah Ellis-Petersen

blocks.text: Hannah Ellis-Petersen

The Red Cross has said at least 93,000 people may have been affected by Wednesday’s flash floods on the Nepal-Tibet border, which have killed more than 540 people, left another 1,500 missing, and triggered a huge rescue operation that is being hampered by fears of new flooding.

The International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies (IFRC), the world’s largest humanitarian network, said it feared the death toll would continue to rise as some of the hardest-hit areas remained inaccessible after roads and bridges were destroyed by the torrents.
“The trauma of this event is enormous,” David Fisher, the IFRC head of delegation for Nepal, said on Friday.

“Thousands of homes have been destroyed or suffered significant damage. We believe that at least 93,000 people have been affected and are in great need. The death toll is very high and unfortunately likely to continue to rise.”
Number of missing in Nepal after flood rises to 1,924, disaster authority confirms
Nepal’s disaster authority raised sharply the number of missing to 1,924 on Friday, two days after devastating floods that killed at least 579 in the country.

The number of missing includes 517 foreigners, as well as 933 workers on hydropower projects on the rivers where a wall of water powered down on Wednesday morning, according to the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority.
South Asia correspondent Hannah Ellis‑Petersen is on the ground in Bidur, one of the most devastated towns in Nepal, after the deadly flash floods that struck on Wednesday morning.
Most homes were completely washed away when a tide of mud, rocks and debris flooded down the river valley.
Those who survived described clinging on to buildings and trees as the water rushed over them.

articles.title: US arrests far-right provocateur Milo Yiannopoulos
articles.summary: Yiannopoulos, a far-right commentator, was an early supporter of Donald Trump and his immigration crackdown, but they have since fallen out. DHS said he was an "illegal alien" who overstayed his…

image.caption: DHS said Yiannopoulos legally entered the US in 2019 and then 'chose to overstay his welcome' [FILE: Nov 16, 2021]Image: Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images/AFP

blocks.text: US authorities have detained right-wing commentator Milo Yiannopoulos and plan to deport him, the Department of Homeland Security said on Friday.

Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents arrested the British provocateur at New Orleans International Airport on Thursday for overstaying in the US, the department said, describing him as an "illegal alien from the United Kingdom."

"Yiannopoulos was issued a final order of removal by an Immigration Judge on July 22, after failing to show up for his immigration hearing," the agency said. "He will remain in ICE custody pending removal."
ICE directed family and legal representatives to contact the agency’s office in Alexandria, Louisiana, which serves as a deportation hub for international flights.
Far-right activist Laura Loomer, who routinely takes credit for action against those who have fallen out with the US president, posted about the incident shortly after.

"I was the first person to report on the fact that Milo was in the US illegally where he incited violence against President Trump and worked for Marjorie Traitor Greene," Loomer wrote on X, referring to the former US congresswoman Marjorie Taylor Greene who stepped down after a feud with Trump.
Loomer went on to say that she "reported him to ICE and the FBI."
Yiannopoulos previously supported ICE
Once a Donald Trump supporter and advocate of the president's immigration crackdown, Yiannopoulos has since fallen out with the Trump movement.
Yiannopoulos first gained notoriety in the early 2010s as a writer for the right-wing website Breitbart News, where he played a key role in the "Gamergate" anti-feminist harassment campaign.
He resigned from Breitbart in 2017 after a video of him appearing to condone pedophilia resurfaced online. He later apologized for the remarks.
Yiannopoulos has continued to espouse far-right views, including calling for a stop to immigration and mass deportations.

As recently as June last year, he said California "needs ICE checkpoints at supermarket entrances, gas stations, strip malls, intersections ​and government buildings, with on the ⁠spot deportation for anyone who can't prove they are in the US legally."

Celebrity news website TMZ suggested that Yiannopoulos may have been in New Orleans ahead of a scheduled performance by Ye, the rapper formerly known as Kanye West. Yiannopoulos has worked for Ye in various capacities, first as part of his aborted 2024 presidential campaign, followed by a brief stint at fashion label Yeezy, and most recently as a personal spokesperson.
Edited by: Sean Sinico

articles.title: Roblox agrees on child-safety measures with PH gov’t
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — Roblox has agreed to integrate stricter safeguards and child protection into its user verification in a bid to prevent the presence of online groomers, the Cybercrime…

blocks.caption: This illustration photo shows a child playing a video game on a tablet using Roblox, an online gaming and game-creation platform, in Terville, northeastern France, on March 11, 2026. —Photo by Jean-Christophe Verhaegen/Agence France-Presse

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — Roblox has agreed to integrate stricter safeguards and child protection into its user verification in a bid to prevent the presence of online groomers, the Cybercrime Investigation and Coordinating Center (CICC) said on Friday.

At a meeting with Philippine officials and Roblox’s executives in Singapore, Roblox committed to incorporating the Philippine National Identification System into its user verification process, CICC said.
Meanwhile, stricter safeguards on its messaging features for children will also be developed, which will ensure minors can only communicate within their age group.

“We are pleased with the direction of our discussions with Roblox and the willingness they have shown to work with the Philippine government. This is an important beginning, and we want to build on it to create a safer gaming environment for our children,” CICC Executive Director Undersecretary Renato Paraiso said.

According to the CICC, Roblox has also implemented an Artificial Intelligence age verification. Users who fail to undergo an age check will have their chat function disabled and will also be restricted to the platform’s kids’ catalog.
It added that Roblox is set to establish an office space in the country by October for a more coordinated response regarding online safety concerns and other matters on its regulations.
A liaison officer will also be designated to directly coordinate with the authorities, including with the National Bureau of Investigation.

“Regulations work best when we understand how these platforms actually operate. We want to hear from the developers, learn what they are seeing on the ground, and use those insights to build safety measures that have teeth, practical, and responsive to new risks,” he expressed.

Meanwhile, Meta has also expressed its support in coordinating with the Philippine government in integrating child protection features and formulating a framework for heightened security measures against online risks.

“The commitments made today are a starting point. The responsibility now is to turn them into action and to ensure that online threats are addressed before they become real-world harm,” Department of Information and Communications Technology (DICT) Secretary Henry Aguda, who was also present at the meeting, said.
The efforts came amid urgent calls for online safeguards for children following the Zamboanga school shooting last Aug. 18.
The Department of Interior and Local Government alleged that the junior high school perpetrator may have been influenced by the game platform after he was found using Roblox. /cb

articles.title: Ombudsman files new graft, malversation raps vs Zaldy Co, others
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — The Office of the Ombudsman on Friday filed a second malversation case against former Ako Bicol party-list Rep. Zaldy Co before the Sandiganbayan over the alleged non-existent…

blocks.caption: Former Rep. Zaldy Co (File photo)

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — The Office of the Ombudsman on Friday filed a second malversation case against former Ako Bicol party-list Rep. Zaldy Co before the Sandiganbayan over the alleged non-existent flood control project worth ₱77 million in Balagtas, Bulacan.

The six-page case information was filed before the anti-graft court for one count each of malversation of public funds and one count each of violation of Republic Act No. 3019, or the Anti-Graft and Corrupt Practices Act against Co as well as former Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH) officials Brice Hernandez, Arjay Salvador Domasig, Jaypee De Leon Mendoza, Niño Lawrence Vergara Morales, Juanito Coronel Mendoza, Floralyn Yutuc Simbulan and Christina Mae Del Rosario Pineda.
They also said that Co’s staff John Paul Estrada and Mark Tecsay “were also included in the indictment.”

The case involves the construction of a riverbank protection structure along the Balagtas River in Purok 4, Barangay San Juan which was awarded to SYMS Construction Trading with a revised contract amount of approximately ₱77.2 million.
Investigators said the project was supposed to begin last Feb. 24, 2025 and was declared to completed on May 2 the same year.
“However, upon inspection, it was non-existent,” the Ombudsman’s ruling said.

The resolution noted that repeated approvals of the payments to SYMS, “in spite of the glaring irregularities” in the Monthly Certificates of Payment and Statements of Work Accomplished “are strong indication of their participation in the devious schemes of misappropriating the funds for flood control projects.”

“Here, respondents acted with evident bad faith and/or gross inexcusable negligence when they issued the pertinent documents and certifications that led to the diversion of public funds … for a project that turned out to be non-existent or incomplete,” the resolution stated.
“The repeated failure to exercise due diligence is very telling.”

In November 2025, Co was charged with one count of malversation and two counts of graft before the Sandiganbayan stemming from a P289.4 million worth Sunwest project — or the company where Co is said to be a beneficial owner — in Naujan, Oriental Mindoro, which prosecutors said was found to have serious structural deficiencies.
Co could not participate in the trial of his first malversation case held in the anti-graft court’s Sixth Division as he was earlier declared by Sandiganbayan as a fugitive from justice.
A respondent declared as a fugitive from justice could not participate in the proceedings and could not seek any judicial relief unless they surrender voluntarily. /gsg

articles.title: Berlin is being blackmailed by hackers, mayor says
articles.summary: Kai Wegner says the German capital and city-state would not cave in to a ransom demand for data stolen in a cyber-attack.

blocks.text: Berlin is being blackmailed by hackers who were able to compromise city systems and steal data earlier this month, its mayor has said.

Kai Wegner said officials would not cave in to the ransom demand, which came on Thursday evening. He did not say how much was being sought, though Der Spiegel reports the hackers are demanding 30 bitcoin, worth around €2m (£1.7m).
Some of the German capital's online systems were forced to close down as a result of the attack, while investigators were working to understand what data had been taken.
The Rhysida group, which is thought to operate from Russia and eastern Europe, and was behind a previous attack on the British Museum, has reportedly taken responsibility.
It has said on its website it intends to begin auctioning the 5.79 terabytes of data it was able to steal from Berlin in seven days' time, according to news agency Reuters.
"Berlin will not be blackmailed," Wegner said on Friday.

He said state police, prosecutors and federal security services were working to investigate the suspected perpetrators "with the utmost urgency", adding that inquiries into the "content and scope of the compromised data are being pursued with great intensity".
Officials for the city-state said an initial data leak occurred between 7 and 12 August.
Then, on 14 August, two department networks were shut down, making applications for housing benefits and payments impossible for several days.
Forensic investigations had since revealed further data leaks within Berlin's transport and environment department, officials said.
"It cannot be ruled out that personal or other non-public data may also be affected," the mayor's office said in a statement on Friday.

Authorities in the capital have not named the suspected cyber-attackers, though Der Spiegel is carrying a screenshot of the Rhysida group's dark web site claiming to possess files including contracts, non-disclosure agreements, personnel files, passwords and thousands of personal contact details.

It is also displaying a countdown, after which it says it will begin auctioning off the data with a starting price of 30 bitcoin - the same amount of the cryptocurrency being sought from Berlin, the German newspaper reports.
The Rhysida group has claimed hundreds of attacks since it emerged in 2023, studies say, and the group has targeted government insititutions and businesses of varying sizes in numerous countries.
It successfully infiltrated the British Museum's computer systems in 2023, disrupting services and stealing around 500,000 files.
When the UK institution refused to pay the ransom, the group published the files - containing the personal data of visitors, subscribers and staff - on the dark web.
The Berlin cyber-attack comes roughly a month before the city holds elections, though state senator Iris Spranger insisted that election infrastructure had not been compromised.

articles.title: Spain asks EU's Frontex for help in processing Ceuta migrants
articles.summary: Of the over 70,000 migrants who illegally crossed into Ceuta from Morocco in late July, some 5,000 still remain in the Spanish exclave. Ceuta residents have been angrily protesting their continued…

image.caption: Some Ceuta residents have attacked tents set up by the migrants along the beachImage: Antonio Sempere/AFP

blocks.text: Spain has asked for help from the European Border and Coast Guard Agency (Frontex) in processing migrants who crossed into Ceuta last month and still remain in the North African Spanish territory.

Spanish Interior Minister Fernando Grande-Marlaska sent a request to Beate Gminder, the European Commission's director general for migration and home affairs, to help with screening migrants in Ceuta.
Madrid has also requested 10 more Frontex officers to help with the screening.
Frontex is the European Union agency responsible for managing the bloc's external borders and fighting cross-border crime.
Why is Spain asking for help with the Ceuta migrants?
Over 70,000 migrants crossed from Morocco to Ceuta illegally in late July. The incident triggered a massive EU migration emergency and brought Spain's leftist government much criticism.
Though the majority of people were quickly sent back to Morocco, at least 5,000 migrants still remain in the Spanish territory of roughly 80,000 residents.
Madrid cannot deport the remaining migrants quickly as a collective return without individual assessment is prohibited under international law and Spanish court rulings.
Unaccompanied minors at risk of sexual assault in Ceuta
Rising anger against migrants in Ceuta
Ceuta's residents loudly reject the migrants' continued presence and have made their voice heard via protests which have sometimes turned violent.
Spain has ruled out moving the migrants into the mainland as that would invite further criticism from the opposition as well as some EU members.
Migrants have set up camp on Trampolin Beach, where some tents have been attacked and set on fire amid the residents' rising anger.

On Thursday, protests turned violent with 12 migrants arrested after stoning an army vehicle, injuring one soldier and other migrants. Spanish newspaper El Pais reported that 11 migrants were expelled from the territory, citing sources from the city's main court.

articles.title: 97-year-old woman rescued after Nepali floods looked like 'a warrior'
articles.summary: A 97-year-old woman, Guna Maya Bohara, survived the flash floods and was rescued using an excavator.

blocks.text: A 97-year-old woman pulled from flood debris in Nepal is recovering in hospital, according to her doctors.
Guna Maya Bohara's great-nephew, Dipak Bohara, has told BBC Nepali she looked like "a warrior" who had returned victorious from battle.
The operation to pull Bohara out of the rubble of her care home took four hours.
Bohara travelled from Kathmandu to help rescue his great-aunt.
Hundreds of people have been confirmed dead after Wednesday's flash floods, which scientists believe were triggered by a glacier collapsing in the Himalayan border region with Tibet.
Video produced by Mansi Kapur and Kamal Pariyar. Video edited by Suneth Perera, Jasmin Dyer and Andrew Webb.

articles.title: Right-wing commentator Milo Yiannopoulos detained by ICE
articles.summary: The British citizen, who lives and works in the US, has supported Trump and ICE agents in the past.

blocks.text: British right-wing political commentator Milo Yiannopoulos has been detained by Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and is awaiting deportation.
Yiannopoulos, 41, a former editor of Breitbart News and onetime employee of rapper Kanye West, appears to be held in Louisiana, according to ICE's inmate registry.

The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) said he "was issued a final order of removal by an Immigration Judge on July 22, after failing to show up for his immigration hearing", and will remain in custody pending deportation.
The self-styled provocateur has called himself the "most fabulous supervillain on the internet". His critics call him a purveyor of hate speech.
Yiannopoulos, who grew up in Kent in the south of England, was arrested on 27 August after arriving at the airport in New Orleans.
He flew into the US in May 2019 and "chose to overstay his welcome in violation of our nation's laws", said DHS.
The DHS statement referred to him as "an illegal alien from the United Kingdom".
The BBC has asked the British embassy in Washington for comment. Yiannopoulos did not respond to the BBC's request for comment.
"Being in detention is a choice," the DHS statement continued, calling on migrants who are in the US illegally to "self-deport now".
Yiannopoulos was an early supporter of Donald Trump during the 2016 election, headlining an event that year called Gays for Trump during the Republican National Convention.

But he soon fell out with the movement. Yiannopoulos still voices support for the Republican president's agenda. But he posted in March this year on X that Trump "has lost his way, bought off by foreign interests".

Yiannopoulos has courted controversy with his comments on transgender people, Muslims, Black Lives Matter, feminists and gay people, even though he himself identified as gay. He now calls himself an "ex-gay".
He has written columns titled "Birth Control Makes Women Unattractive and Crazy" and "Would You Rather Your Child Had Feminism or Cancer?"
He has also cheered on ICE raids, writing on X last year: "Total legal immunity for ICE agents when they're on duty."
He posted in 2025: "We have got to deport millions and millions of people. Without that, nothing else matters."
Yiannopoulos also advocated on social media for "on the spot deportation for anyone who can't prove they are in the US legally".

In 2017, he was uninvited from speaking at CPAC, a US conservative conference that also hosted Trump, after footage emerged of Yiannopoulos appearing to condone paedophilia. He also later apologised and resigned from Breitbart.
He denied the allegations, and said he had been speaking about his own experiences as a child.
Yiannopoulos was once regularly linked with the alt-right, a disparate group that is outspoken against political correctness and feminism and which includes neo-Nazis and white supremacists.
He has said he does not consider himself part of the alt-right, although he has called it "energising and exciting".

articles.title: How and why CBC News will adjust its 9/11 language guidance
articles.summary: CBC’s reporting on terrorism, wherever it occurs, has always been guided by the principle of attribution, and like other major news organizations, it has been our practice for decades.

image.caption: Confusion has been swirling about how CBC News journalists use the words 'terrorist' and 'terrorism,' particularly in connection with the al-Qaeda attacks on New York, Washington, D.C., and Pennsylvania on Sept. 11, 2001. (Spencer Platt/Getty Images)

blocks.text: Editor's Blog
CBC’s reporting on terrorism, wherever it occurs, has always been guided by the principle of attribution, and like other major news organizations, it has been our practice for decades.
Attribution no longer required for describing Sept. 11 attacks as terrorism
We use this editor's blog to explain our journalism and what's happening at CBC News. You can find more blog posts here.

CBC News finds itself once again in a swirl of confusion about how our journalists use the words "terrorist" and "terrorism," this time about the al-Qaeda attacks on New York, Washington, D.C., and Pennsylvania on Sept. 11, 2001.

The confusion stems from the leak of an excerpt from our internal language guide that was published and amplified by a number of outlets without full context or explanation. It has caused significant concern, anger and hurt for many people who believe CBC News seeks to minimize or obscure the horror of that day and who was behind it.

That is the last thing we want to do. And our reporting on 9/11, through thousands of stories over the past 25 years, is an unflinching account of the devastating attacks by al-Qaeda, the hunt and prosecution of those responsible, the thousands of lives that were lost on that day and the incalculable loss and grief experienced by so many others as a result.
And we intend to mark the forthcoming 25th anniversary of 9/11 with extensive, special coverage that will continue to respectfully and thoughtfully reflect on the monumental nature of this tragedy.

CBC's reporting on terrorism, wherever it occurs, has always been guided by the principle of attribution, and like other major news organizations, it has been our practice for decades. The reason for the extreme care around the use of the words "terrorist" and "terrorism" was detailed in this earlier editor's blog.

But to be clear, CBC News has never said what happened on Sept. 11, 2001, was not terrorism, as some commentators have stated in recent days. We have reported fully and accurately on the reasons and motivations for those attacks as determined by police, governments and an independent commission. We've just made sure to do it with attribution.
Clarity and understanding are at the heart of our journalism. The leaked excerpt without context or explanation has raised more questions for the public that we must now answer.
After reviewing our current language guidance, we have decided to adjust it to clarify that direct attribution is not required for describing the historic events of 9/11 as terrorism.
We are doing so to remove what has unfortunately (and unintentionally) become an impediment to clarity and public understanding.

At the same time, as new acts of politically or ideologically motivated violence occur in our world, we will continue to follow the journalistically sound practice of attributing causes and motivations to officials and experts.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Basem Boshra
Senior director of journalistic standards and public trust

Basem Boshra is the senior director of journalistic standards and public trust at CBC News. He was previously the director of journalism and programming for CBC Quebec (English Services) from 2022 to 2025. Before joining CBC, Basem spent more than 20 years at the Montreal Gazette, where he held key leadership roles including deputy editor, managing editor, digital editor, city editor, and columnist. His career also includes positions at CTV News Montreal, the National Post and Dose Magazine.

articles.title: Andreescu, fellow Canadian Draxl lose in final round of U.S. Open qualifying
articles.summary: No Canadians will enter the singles draws at the U.S. Open through the qualifying tournament after Bianca Andreescu and Liam Draxl lost in final round action Friday in New York.

image.caption: From left: Bianca Andreescu, the 2019 women's U.S. Open champion, fell 2-6, 6-3, 6-4 to Slovenia's Tamara Zidansek in the final qualifying round Friday, while fellow Canadian Liam Draxl dropped a 4-6, 7-5, 7-6 (7) decision to Australia's Tristan Schoolkate. (Dave Shopland/Associated Press, Minas Pan

blocks.text: Tennis·ROUNDUP
No Canadians will enter the singles draws at the U.S. Open through the qualifying tournament after Bianca Andreescu and Liam Draxl lost in final round action Friday in New York.
Teammates Auger-Aliassime and Shapovalov in men's main draw that begins Sunday

Andreescu fell 2-6, 6-3, 6-4 to Slovenia's Tamara Zidansek. The 2019 U.S. Open women's champion from Mississauga, Ont., fired seven aces across the two-hour 44-minute match but struggled on net points, winning just 10 of the 21 available.
The match started Thursday but had to be suspended due to rain. Andreescu was up 2-0 at the time.
Draxl of Newmarket, Ont., also had his qualifying match against Australia's Tristan Schoolkate pushed to Friday before losing 4-6, 7-5, 7-6 (7).

items: Andreescu, Branstine advance to U.S. Open final qualifying round
Andreescu bounced from NBO, compatriot Kayla Cross secures 1st WTA win

blocks.text: Both players scored four breaks, but Schoolkate was the last to win against serve to go up 4-3 in the third set and erase an early Draxl advantage.

Montreal's Felix Auger-Aliassime and Denis Shapovalov of Richmond Hill, Ont., will be on the men's side when main draw action begins Sunday, while 2021 runner-up Leylah Fernandez of Laval, Que., will be on the women's side.
Sabalenka, Pegula want prize money boost, new player council

Aryna Sabalenka ​and Jessica Pegula praised the U.S. Open's record prize money allocation and the creation of a Grand Slam player advisory council, saying calls for competitors to get a larger share of the revenue were beginning to gain traction.

The U.S. Open announced a ‌record $108 million US prize purse for this year's tournament, while the four Grand Slams unveiled plans for an advisory council following growing pressure from leading players for increased prize money and a bigger role in decisions affecting the sport.
World No. 1 Sabalenka, a ​vocal supporter of efforts to improve player compensation, said ​the developments could help ease tensions between players and tournament organizers.
"We're super happy … that we're finally getting to the point where we wanted to be at ​the very beginning," the Belarusian told reporters on Friday.

items: Djokovic-Sabalenka, Williams-Alcaraz suffer first-round losses in U.S. Open mixed doubles

blocks.text: "Hopefully we're not gonna boycott ⁠media or tournament or anything ⁠in the future. We all going to be ‌happy, and that's all we wanted from the very beginning."

Sabalenka and men's world No. 1 Jannik Sinner were among the top players who limited their pre-tournament media availabilities at the French Open and Wimbledon this year to 15 minutes as part of ⁠a protest to demand a higher percentage of tournament revenue for prize money.
Unity helped in player council talks
The 15-minute limit was intended to symbolize the roughly 15 per cent of tournament revenue that the tournaments allocated to player prize money.

items: More tennis coverage

blocks.text: American Pegula, ‌who has taken on a leadership role in discussions involving players and tennis' governing bodies, said unity between the men's and women's tours had helped produce tangible progress.

"I think it's been amazing what the players have been able to accomplish," Pegula said. "They have never ​had anything like this as far as with the slams being able to generate a council, also the player welfare contribution, ⁠and then another increase in prize money."
The world No. 3 said the initiatives reflected sustained pressure from ⁠players as they seek a greater voice in a sport long criticized for its fragmented ⁠structure.
With files from Reuters

articles.title: Austria museum heist: Thieves snatch diamond necklace
articles.summary: The stolen necklace, studded with 673 precious stones, belonged to Egypt's Queen Nazli. It was being displayed as part of the museum's exhibition for designs by France's Van Cleef and Arpels.

image.caption: The two robbers bought tickets to enter the MAK museum. But once inside, they 'smashed a glass display case' with a hammer and fled with the priceless jewelry, police has saidImage: Jeremy Audouard/AFP

blocks.text: Two men walked into Vienna's Museum of Applied Arts (MAK) as visitors only to storm out with a priceless 200-carat platinum and diamond necklace worth several million dollars, police said on Friday.
The broad-daylight heist on Thursday, the latest in a series of high-profile thefts to have hit European museums in the past year, triggered a search that grew beyond Austria's borders.
What do we know about the heist?
The two robbers bought tickets to enter the museum.

But once inside, they made their way to the temporary exhibition for French designers Van Cleef and Arpels and "smashed a glass display case" with a hammer before "fleeing with the jewelry in an unknown direction," according to a police statement.
Police added that they did not wear masks and could be clearly seen on surveillance cameras.
A police spokeswoman told the German DPA news agency that one of the robbers was carrying what is believed to be a real firearm.
She said visitors and security staff were in the room when the display case was smashed, adding that it was understandable that the security staff did not stand in the way of the armed perpetrator.
The MAK museum confirmed the theft but did not comment further. On its website, the museum continues to promote its exhibition, which is due to run until September 27.

blocks.caption: The stolen necklace, made of platinum and 673 precious stones said to weigh over 200 carats, was designed for Egypt's last royal familyImage: Landespolizeidirektion Wien/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: What do we know about the stolen necklace?

The stolen necklace belonged to Egypt's now-deposed Queen Nazli and was designed for her in 1939 for her daughter's marriage to the future Shah of Iran, Mohammad Reza Pahlavi, whose family has also since been removed from power.
It is made of platinum and 673 precious stones said to weigh over 200 carats.
Van Cleef and Arpels describes the necklace on its website as a "triumph of white jewelry."
The case is only the latest in a string of heists to have hit European museums in recent month.

The most high profile was last October's Louvre museum break-in in Paris, which saw thieves snatching in jewellery worth $102 million (roughly €88 million) in under eight minutes. Museum thefts have also been reported in Italy and Spain.
France: 2,500-year-old necklace stolen from museum
Edited by: Sean Sinico
