articles.title: King Haakon begins reign after turbulent year for Norwegian monarchy
articles.summary: Haakon becomes the king at a turbulent time for Norway's monarchy.

blocks.text: Image source, Getty Images
King Haakon VIII has adopted his father's motto "Everything for Norway"
ByJames Gregory and Mallory Moench
King Haakon VIII has inherited the Norwegian throne after the death of his father, Harald V. Many in Norway believe he has big shoes to fill.
King Harald was immensely popular with ordinary Norwegians, as shown by his consistent high polling and the outpouring of emotion in the lead-up to his death.
Haakon is the fourth king to head Norway's modern monarchy, since it was restored in 1905 after the country gained independence from Sweden.
Among his first duties as monarch, he led an extraordinary cabinet meeting where he announced his royal title and adopted his father's motto "Everything for Norway".
Many commentators believe he is well-placed to follow in his predecessors' footsteps.

As crown prince, Haakon worked closely with his father as he carried out his royal duties and in recent years was handed more responsibility, increasingly acting as regent while Harald was ill or absent.
"I am so lucky that Crown Prince Haakon is the one who will carry this forward," King Harald wrote of his son in his biography The King Tells.
Historian Trond Norén Isaksen tells the BBC that Haakon will be a different type of king to his father, but no less respected.
"King Harald... [was] very charismatic, he [had] a great sense of humour, which everyone appreciates, and Haakon is a bit more reserved, a bit more like his mother.

"But in recent years he has also become a bit more relaxed and opened up a bit and showed a bit more of his sense of humour... he has been pulling enormous weight for many years given his parents have become older and his wife has been ill."
Haakon is a great-great-great-grandson of Britain's Queen Victoria.
His daughter Ingrid Alexandra, 22, now becomes the crown princess and heir to the Norwegian throne.

blocks.caption: Image caption, At the age of 22, Ingrid Alexandra becomes Norway's crown princess

blocks.text: At the age of 22, Ingrid Alexandra becomes Norway's crown princess
Haakon was ahead of his older sister, Princess Märtha Louise, in the line of succession.
The constitution was changed in 1990 to give women the right to inherit the throne, so Crown Princess Ingrid Alexandra is in line to be Norway's first female head of state since the 15th Century.
Haakon has become the king at a turbulent time for Norway's royal family.
The monarchy remains broadly popular among Norwegians and has been long praised for its modern outlook.
But in recent years it has been beset by scandal.

Only this year, Haakon's wife Mette-Marit, now Queen of Norway, has apologised for several years of ties to convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein, and her son has been convicted of rape in a high-profile trial. Marius Borg Høiby, who was born from an earlier relationship, is appealing against the conviction.
Born in 1973, King Haakon is the youngest child of the late king and Queen Sonja.
By Haakon's own admission, he struggled at times to accept his royal status in his early years.
"Yes, I was a royal, but I did not want to talk about it... ​At school it made me anxious," he wrote in his 2023 autobiography, recalling his days in a state primary school in the 1980s.
He became crown prince in 1991 at the tender age of 17, following the death of his grandfather King Olav V.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Three generations of monarch at the family's Skaugum estate in 1982 - King Olav V, with the young Prince Haakon and then-Crown Prince Harald

blocks.text: Image source, EPA
Three generations of monarch at the family's Skaugum estate in 1982 - King Olav V, with the young Prince Haakon and then-Crown Prince Harald
Unusually for a royal, he was educated at local state schools before embarking upon a four-year-long naval career, graduating from the Norwegian Naval Academy in 1995.
He decided not to follow his father and grandfather to Oxford University, instead flying to California to enrol at the University of Berkeley, where he studied political science.
Soon after his return to Norway, Haakon met his now-wife Mette-Marit at a music festival in her home city of Kristiansand in 1999.
She was dubbed by the press as the Cinderella of Kristiansand - a reference to her humble beginnings.
"What we two found together was so strong that I could not let it go," the then-Crown Prince Haakon said of Mette-Marit ahead of their wedding in 2001.
But their relationship was not without controversy and there was a fierce public debate in Norway from the moment Haakon first announced they were dating.

Some commentators even warned at the time that their relationship could spell the end of the Norwegian monarchy, with comparisons being made to the infamous union between American divorcee Wallis Simpson and British King Edward VIII which led to his abdication in 1936.
Queen Mette-Marit was not the first commoner to marry into the Norwegian royal family - the late King Harald had already broken with tradition by marrying Queen Sonja three decades earlier.
She was, however, a single mother to a four-year-old child whose father had served time for a conviction of cocaine possession.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Crown Princess Sonja, Princess Märtha Louise, Prince Haakon and Crown Prince Harald at Skaugum in 1987

blocks.text: Crown Princess Sonja, Princess Märtha Louise, Prince Haakon and Crown Prince Harald at Skaugum in 1987

The royal couple's co-habitation in an Oslo flat had also drawn criticism from the conservative Lutheran Church of Norway - though polls from the time showed most ordinary Norwegians did not care about either.
What many Norwegians did question, though, was whether her former party lifestyle was one compatible with that of someone married to the future king.

In an emotional interview three days before their marriage, Mette-Marit publicly apologised for her "wild past" and condemned drug use after reports that drugs were taken at parties she attended in Oslo during the 1990s.
She did not say whether she had taken them herself.
It was seen as something of a turning point. She won the affection of ordinary Norwegians and for years has been seen as the embodiment of a modern monarchy capable of shaking up convention.
The couple have two children together, Ingrid and Prince Sverre Magnus.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Haakon and Mette-Marit married in August 2001

blocks.text: Haakon and Mette-Marit married in August 2001
In her new role as crown princess, she took up popular causes including support for people with HIV and promoting literacy.
Her diagnosis with pulmonary fibrosis in 2018 also led to widespread public sympathy.

Haakon has said Mette-Marit helped him come out of his shell and described her as an emotional counterweight to his analytical mind. "I am not very good socially," he wrote. "Mette is a natural talent. She can go into a room and get along with everyone."
But in recent times, Haakon's family has come under increasingly heavy public scrutiny and criticism.
Marius Borg Høiby's rape conviction hangs over the family. One of women was raped on Haakon's estate at Skaugum outside Oslo.
Høiby has always been treated as one of the family, although the royal house has repeatedly stressed he is not a royal.
Days before his trial began, documents were released revealing Mette-Marit's frequent contact with late sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.

She later apologised to King Harald and Queen Sonja for her three-year friendship with Epstein and admitted to "poor judgement", adding in a national TV interview that she wished she had never met him.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Haakon's family affairs have been the subject of media and public scrutiny in recent times

blocks.text: Haakon's family affairs have been the subject of media and public scrutiny in recent times
Several polls conducted earlier this year found nearly half of Norway's population felt the crown princess could not become queen, even though it was always bound to happen.
Two days after her son's trial came to an end, Mette-Marit received a lung transplant, eight years after her initial diagnosis.
Her doctors will not declare her stable until a year after the transplant, and the new king will face a difficult period of succession as he continues to support her.

Caroline Vagle, royal correspondent for Se og Hør magazine, says in regards to Epstein the most important thing the royal family can do is be "completely open about what actually happened, and not allow public speculation to take on a life of its own".
"But I also don't think we should overestimate the impact of one or two difficult cases," she says.
"What will ultimately matter is how the royal family handles them, and how Haakon and the next generation manage to build on the trust that Harald has earned over a lifetime."
Tove Taalesen, royal correspondent for Nettavisen, believes the scandals will be challenging but Haakon is "very much ready for the task".
"I'm sure that in the future he will be respected and loved, similar to King Haakon VII, King Olav V and also King Harald V."
Haakon's reign begins in the backdrop of these scandals, and how he navigates them might come to define his monarchy.

articles.title: Nepal-Tibet flood rescue efforts resume after being halted by overflowing lake
articles.summary: Risk of fresh flooding had forced rescue teams to withdraw as residents rushed up hills to escape possible river surge
articles.byline: Hannah Ellis-Petersen in Bidur, Sam Jones and agencies

blocks.text: Rescuers searching for survivors of deadly flash floods on the Nepal-Tibet border have resumed their efforts after suspending operations when a debris dam burst its bank on Friday, increasing the risk of fresh flooding.

Residents in Nepal’s Rasuwa district, on the border with Tibet, were seen rushing up hillsides ⁠on Friday to escape a possible surge in the river, ⁠according to witnesses. Fears of another flood came as authorities in Nepal and China said that at least 543 people had been killed in the disaster.

blocks.caption: Barrier lake forms at base of mountains near Nepal border

blocks.text: More than 500 foreign citizens were among 826 people missing in Nepal, police and tourism ⁠officials said, including 177 from India, 90 from the US, 34 from Australia, 33 from Britain and 25 from Canada. Chinese state media said at least 558 were missing on the Tibet side of the border, of whom at least 260 were foreign nationals.
The flood on Wednesday had destroyed power stations, roads and bridges along a route that links Kathmandu with Lhasa in Tibet and is ⁠popular with trekkers and pilgrims.

The Chinese state broadcaster CCTV reported that a lake formed by piles of debris from the mudslide had begun overflowing on Friday, sending water towards the area where rescue teams were headed, and forcing a brief pause in operations.

Rescue efforts in Bidur, the capital of the Nuwakot district in Bagmati province, Nepal, were disrupted on Friday morning as the the Trishuli River began to rise again after the lake near the China border burst its banks.
Rescue workers were moved from the area and people who had tried to return to what remained of their homes were told to evacuate again immediately.

Bidur, once a bustling town on the banks of the Trishuli, now lies in ruins. Most homes were washed away when a tide of mud, rocks and debris surged down the river valley early on Wednesday. Survivors described clinging to buildings and trees as the water rushed over them.

The mangled concrete remains of a bank, a government office and an ATM booth were among the few structures left standing, although they were submerged in mud. Officials said there were still bodies inside the buildings but it was too dangerous to recover them.
Nearby, local people gathered along the muddy road, calling out for lost relatives and trying to dig out what was left of their belongings.

Most areas battered by flash floods remained accessible only by army helicopter. At the Bidur army camp, where much of the rescue effort was being coordinated, rescue and military helicopters flew in and out every five minutes, bringing in dozens of traumatised victims. Many said that in a matter of minutes, the floods had taken their loved ones, their homes and everything they owned.
The international community is scrambling to get aid to flood-stricken parts of Nepal and Tibet.

blocks.caption: Sludge inundates homes after flash floods in Nuwakot district. Photograph: AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: Nepal has said it does not yet need foreign assistance as the search-and-rescue operation – complicated by the destruction of dozens of bridges and miles of roads across the mountainous region – continues.

“The offer for help is natural,” Lok Bahadur Chhetri, a spokesperson for Nepal’s foreign ministry, said on Friday. “Our security agencies ‌are doing the search and rescue operation. For now we don’t require such help.”

The Kathmandu Post reported that India, China, the US, Britain, Japan, South Korea, Sri Lanka and Bangladesh had asked the government to allow their search-and-rescue teams to assist in the operation.
after newsletter promotion

Dinesh Bhattarai, a former Nepali ⁠ambassador to the UN in Geneva, said the government’s reluctance to ​accept foreign assistance may ​be linked to sensitivities over ​Rasuwa district and its border with China’s Tibet region.
“They may have thought about ​the locational sensitivity ‌of the region and ​decided not to ​accept foreign teams,” Bhattarai told Reuters.
But Chhetri said Nepal’s own rescue teams were handling the operation and the decision to refuse foreign assistance had nothing to do with sensitivities involving China.

Scant information has emerged from Chinese authorities about the scale of the destruction in Tibet, the most tightly controlled part of China even under normal circumstances. Only brief, state-controlled media reports about the floods have been allowed to circulate in China and the authorities have confirmed only three deaths there. Chinese reports have focused on rescue efforts.
In Nepal earlier on Friday, army helicopter rescue teams were working to free about 100 people trapped in a tunnel at a flooded hydropower project.
“Our focus is in search and rescue of people … some people are trapped in the tunnel of Trishuli 3A hydropower project,” said the Nepal army spokesperson, Raja Ram Basnet.

“Two helicopters have been dispatched but it is challenging because it is tough to even locate the entry points of the tunnel. Relief efforts are also under way to provide the rescued people what they need.”
The prime minister’s office said the army was working in challenging conditions and had rescued 350 workers and local people who were trapped in the tunnel.

Rescue teams reported finding bodies hundreds of miles downstream from the disaster zone in the Chitwan district of Nepal, near the Tibetan border. Dozens of injured people were transported to Kathmandu for advanced medical care and more than 100 people were rescued by Nepali army personnel in helicopters.
CCTV said 499 Chinese nationals and 555 foreigners had been transported out of the disaster zone as of Friday.
With Agence France-Presse and Reuters

articles.title: Why Germany's military is betting on gamers
articles.summary: For the past 10 years, the German armed forces — the Bundeswehr — have been represented at Gamescom, Cologne's video game trade fair. They've been criticized for trying to draw more young people into…

image.caption: The Bundeswehr will once again be represented at the Gamescom video game trade fair in Cologne in 2026Image: Kristina Reymann-Schneider/DW

blocks.text: Gamescom, which runs from August 26-30 in Cologne, is promoted as the world's largest video game trade show.

Last year, two-thirds of its non-industry visitors were male, with over 40% of them between the ages of 16 and 25. Those are precisely the young people the Bundeswehr, Germany's armed forces, is trying to reach as it urgently seeks to expand its ranks.

Germany's military aims to have 260,000 active-duty soldiers by 2035. The German government has supplied hundreds of billions of euros to modernize the country's armed forces. Defense has become a priority for Germany in the face of the current global security situation.
Career advice in camouflage
The Bundeswehr set up shop at Gamescom for the first time in 2016. It's been back every year since.

A brand-new, olive-green Caracal off-road vehicle is one of the main attractions. Alongside it are laptops belonging to the Bundeswehr's Center for Cyber Operations — tasked with cyber defense, among other responsibilities.
Under a watchful eye, visitors can try their hand at hacking.

blocks.caption: The Caracal off-road vehicle is a popular photo opportunity at the Bundeswehr boothImage: Kristina Reymann-Schneider/DW

blocks.text: At another station, visitors can put on VR headsets to get a glimpse into the working life of a soldier aboard a naval vessel. Pilots, aircraft mechanics and air traffic controllers present their professions in a 3D experience. Elsewhere, several fit mountain infantry soldiers stand beside a pull-up bar, where visitors are invited to test their strength.

New this year is a career lounge where interested visitors can have what the Bundeswehr is calling "career counseling sessions." The atmosphere is positive, with soldiers promoting their jobs without being pushy, taking time to answer questions from visitors — who have primarily come to Gamescom to have fun, meet friends and play the latest games.
Do gamers make good soldiers?

A representative study by Germany's Bitkom digital association found that one in five people found it likely that video and computer games teach skills that could be useful in wartime — training reaction speed and problem-solving, for instance. However, being a good gamer doesn't necessarily make for a good soldier.

blocks.caption: Lieutenant General Robert Sieger, president of the Federal Office for Bundeswehr Personnel ManagementImage: Kristina Reymann-Schneider/DW

blocks.text: "We need people who are comfortable with technology," Lt. Gen. Robert Sieger, president of the Federal Office for Bundeswehr Personnel Management, told DW. "What we don't want are people who think we're playing an ego shooter or some kind of shooting game. That doesn't do justice to the seriousness of the situation at all. War isn't a game. As a soldier and a general, it is important to me that people understand the seriousness of what we do."

For Sieger, educating people about the Bundeswehr and the range of careers it offers is a central reason for having a booth at Gamescom. "We're an integral part of our country's safety net. We have to simply be here and show what it means to stand up for the freedom of our country, be that as a soldier or a civilian."
Criticism of Bundeswehr presence
The Bundeswehr is represented alongside many other employers in the gaming trade show's Job Area, including Germany's federal police, retailer Edeka and software company DATEV.

Gamescom is, however, still a video game trade show — and not everyone is comfortable with the Bundeswehr getting close to the gaming world. The German Peace Society — United War Resisters has criticized the Bundeswehr presence at Gamescom, along with booths operated by Germany's foreign intelligence service and defense companies such as Airbus and Rheinmetall.

blocks.caption: 'Level Up for Your Career': Peace activists criticize the Bundeswehr's use of gaming jargonImage: Kristina Reymann-Schneider/DW

blocks.text: Peace campaigner Marius Pletsch says the Bundeswehr uses inappropriate slogans, designed to appeal specifically to gamers, and distorts the image of military service.

"We think it's wrong to lure young people to the booth by appealing to their sense of adventure. We don't think the Bundeswehr should be represented at a trade show that is primarily about video games and leisure to boost its personnel numbers," he told DW.
For two days, the peace organization will have a booth outside the trade show exhibition halls, providing information about conscientious objection to military service.
Bundeswehr: Not just any job
"Being a soldier isn't a normal job," the peace initiative said in a statement.
Lt. Gen. Sieger uses similar terms, but puts it somewhat differently: "Being a soldier isn't a job like any other. We put our lives on the line for the security of our people."

He reaches a different conclusion than the peace advocates, though. "It would be downright negligent for an organization responsible for our country's security not to be an inherent part of society," Sieger said. "As an inherent part of society and a modern employer, of course we have our rightful spot here in the Job Area, just as we have over recent years."
What do young Gamescom visitors make of the Bundeswehr's presence?

"Morally questionable, but a good employer," said Dennis, a 22-year-old computer science student, although he said the Bundeswehr wasn't for him. Dominik, 26, said he was pleased that the German military was represented at Gamescom. "You can actually have a pretty good conversation with them. They're all very nice," he said. He said he may even consider working for the Bundeswehr's cyber defense division.
This article was originally written in German.
Hooked on video gaming

articles.title: 'Not far enough' - US parents and teens on Meta's new limits for young users
articles.summary: As part of an $18bn settlement in a child-safety lawsuit, Meta announced new restrictions on its apps. We asked families what they thought.

blocks.text: For Elizabeth Cardner, a mother of two girls in Houston, Texas, Meta's new limits on how teenagers can use its platforms are a welcome sign that more people are aware of social media's potential dangers.
But, she tells the BBC, they probably won't help much in the long-term.
"It will save a few arguments at home, but it doesn't go far enough," she says.

This week, Meta announced new restrictions on its platforms - which include Instagram, Facebook and Whatsapp - as part of an $18bn (£13.25bn) settlement with US states in a lawsuit on social media's effects on children.

The company said it would set a daily two-hour time limit, hide the number of likes that a post receives, remove autoplay on videos, mute push notifications during school hours, and ban extreme make-up filters.
It also announced changes to its age-verification process and parental controls as well as agreeing to appoint an independent auditor to check the measures are implemented and maintained.

Many parents across the US see the restrictions as helpful, but are still sceptical. Those who spoke to the BBC described feeling stuck - where they feel they can't cut their children off from social media but also can't protect them from the harms they believe it causes - and they are waiting to see how much of a difference these new rules will make.

Cardner's 14-year-old, Paige, believes the restrictions will lead to "more real-life scenarios" and less "fake content", which she says dominates social media. She and her sister both approve of hiding the numbers of likes and restricting filters.
But Paige sees those gains as short-lived, "since AI is evolving".

"People will find new ways to have fake filters, and correct certain parts of their videos or pictures," she says. "So I think it'll help until people use other resources to try and find new ways to do that."
Cardner says banning her daughters entirely from social media would only result in them being left out by their peers.
"Damned if you do, damned if you don't," she says. "I don't think there's any winning on it."

Another mother of two teens, Andria Rose, told the BBC that she feels defenceless and "no matter how much I protect my kids, Facebook, Instagram - they're coming in and literally, like, taking them out of their rooms".
Even though she calls Meta's changes "fantastic", Rose, who lives near Boston, Massachusetts, doesn't believe they are fully addressing the problem.
"They're trying to limit the drug, but they're not controlling the drug," she says. "They're still dealing."
Rose notes her personal use of social media costs her sleep at night.
"I'm hooked," she says. "So what do you think is going to happen to a kid?"
The settlement was announced on Wednesday in the middle of a highly-anticipated trial, where Meta owner Mark Zuckerberg was expected to testify. The settlement did not include any admission of fault.

The lawsuit was originally filed in 2023 by 29 US states, alleging Meta deliberately designed its platforms to be addictive and lied about risks. They also accused it of violating a federal law on collecting children's personal information.
The settlement - announced this week - included 48 states, plus the District of Columbia and three US territories.

Several studies have found social media to be harmful to mental health, especially for children. Last year, a BBC investigation found children were being exposed to content about bullying, suicide and weapons on social media platforms.

For Rose, Meta's settlement payment "is like throwing a couple of dollar bills at a problem", given how much money the company makes and how much she believes the industry profited from children during the pandemic.
Joanie Story, a mother of four boys in Long Island, takes issue with another part of Meta's announcement - its conditions involving other platforms.
The company will withhold $5bn of the settlement, and only release it if YouTube, TikTok and others also enter into similar agreements.
It also said it would further tighten its time limit to one hour if other platforms implement similar restrictions. Story sees that as "petty".
"That's like saying: 'You know, we have the ability to fix what is broken, but we're only gonna fix it halfway,'" she says.

Still, Story is greeting the new rules as "good controls". She says she saw what a lack of controls could do when two of her sons were accidentally exposed to explicit content on a non-Meta platform. One boy has been in therapy for four years, she says.

articles.title: Norway's King Harald dies aged 89: A beloved monarch buffeted by family crises
articles.summary: The late king, who reigned for 35 years, broke with tradition by marrying a commoner and was widely loved by Norwegians.

blocks.text: Watch: A look back at the King who broke with tradition
Norway's King Harald V has died at the age of 89, after he was taken to hospital last week for treatment for a rare blood condition.
The palace in Oslo said he passed away peacefully at 06:35 local time (04:35 GMT) on Friday at the national hospital in Oslo.

The royal flag on the roof of the palace has been lowered to half-mast and a period of national mourning has been declared leading up to the day of his funeral. Crowds of mourners have streamed to the royal palace to lay flowers and flags.
Harald was the nation's first king born there since the 14th Century. He has been succeeded by his son Haakon, 53, who will hold an extraordinary council of state with the government later on Friday.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Harald was Norway's first king born in Norway since the 14th Century

blocks.text: Image source, Anwar Hussein/Getty Images
Harald was Norway's first king born in Norway since the 14th Century

King Charles III sent his "most heartfelt condolences" at the death of his "dear cousin" - who was a second cousin to Queen Elizabeth II - while King Carl XVI Gustaf of Sweden remembered "a good friend to me, my family and to Sweden", wishing his godson Haakon "success and good fortune".

After 35 years on the throne, Harald will be remembered as a popular and reforming figure who modernised the monarchy, broke with tradition by marrying a commoner and served as a unifying figure at Norway's most difficult moments.
Royal observers say he was down-to-earth, respected and beloved, describing him as a "grandfather" of the nation and the "People's king" - a title also used by his father King Olav V.

During his reign, the Norwegian monarchy became more egalitarian and transparent about the royal family's finances and health matters, Ole-Jørgen Schulsrud-Hansen, historian and TV2 royal correspondent, told the BBC.

Tove Taalesen, royal correspondent for Nettavisen, described the late king as "one of us", while Caroline Vagle, royal expert for Se og Hør magazine, said he had "always been very close to the people".
"He has never been afraid to show emotion, humour or vulnerability, and that has made him very human."

blocks.caption: People and children gather in a row alongside flowers and flags on the ground.

blocks.text: Image source, REUTERS/Dylan Martinez
In the wake of the 2011 bomb and gun attacks on Oslo and the island of Utøya, Harald appealed to Norwegians to support each other and not "let fear take over".

More recently, Harald and his family faced health challenges and scandal, especially over his daughter-in-law Mette-Marit's association with the late sex offender Jeffrey Epstein and her son Marius Borg Høiby's conviction for rape.
He is survived by his wife of almost 58 years, Queen Sonja, their daughter Princess Märtha Louise, their son, the new King Haakon, and six grandchildren.

blocks.caption: Image caption, King Harald and Queen Elizabeth II were second cousins

blocks.text: Image source, Dominic Lipinski/PA Wire
King Harald and Queen Elizabeth II were second cousins
Harald was born on 21 February 1937 on the Skaugum estate near Oslo. He was three when dictator Adolf Hitler ordered the Nazi German invasion of Norway early in World War Two.
Harald's mother fled with her children across the border to Sweden, and they travelled to the US on the invitation of President Franklin D Roosevelt.

Prince Harald returned with his family to Norway at the end of the war and completed his school and compulsory military service. He became crown prince in 1957, studying social science, history and economics at Balliol College in Oxford from 1960 to 1962.

He met Sonja Haraldsen, the daughter of a businessman, at a party, but the crown prince had to wait nine years before he was allowed to marry her. Eventually he told his father that if he could not marry Sonja, he would stay single, King Harald once told Norway's public broadcaster, external.
His father finally gave his consent and the couple wed in Oslo Cathedral on 29 August 1968.
Harald's choice paved the way for his own two children to marry commoners too, and for Vagle, that "helped bring an end to a very male-dominated royal family".

blocks.caption: Image caption, (L-R) Prince Sverre Magnus, the new King Haakon, Crown Princess Mette-Marit, Queen Sonja and King Harald of Norway attend Norwegian Constitution Day at the Royal Palace in Oslo in May

blocks.text: Image source, Per Ole Hagen/Getty Images
(L-R) Prince Sverre Magnus, the new King Haakon, Crown Princess Mette-Marit, Queen Sonja and King Harald of Norway attend Norwegian Constitution Day at the Royal Palace in Oslo in May
When his father became ill in 1990, the then-crown prince became regent. Harald then ascended to the throne when Olav died on 17 January 1991.
The new king came into his own around 2000, according to historian Trond Norén Isaksen, growing from a shy man into someone much more open and empathetic.

In July 2011, Harald faced his greatest challenge yet as king, when neo-Nazi Anders Breivik murdered eight people with a car bomb in Oslo before moving onto a youth camp on the island of Utøya, where he shot dead 69 others, most of them teenagers.

He gave a televised address the next day, and weeks later he delivered a speech, empathising with the victims and their families as a father, grandfather, husband and king. On the verge of tears, his voice quivered and broke.
"I can only imagine the depth of your pain. As king of this nation, I feel for each and every one of you," he said.
Looking back, historian Ole-Jørgen Schulsrud-Hansen said: "I think that moment has been burned into our minds of what a monarchy should be."

blocks.caption: A picture taken on August 29, 1968 shows Norway's Crown Prince Harald and Sonja Haraldsen waving as they leave in their car the Oslo Cathedral during their wedding ceremony.

blocks.text: Image source, AFP via Getty Images
In 2016, the king made headlines again by giving a, external speech, external supporting diversity of religion, ethnicity and sexual orientation.

He said Norwegians were from "Afghanistan, Pakistan and Poland, from Sweden, Somalia and Syria", that they "believe in God, Allah, the Universe and nothing", and that they "are girls who love girls, boys who love boys, and girls and boys who love each other".

The king was also a keen athlete and environmentalist - one of the initiators of the Norwegian branch of the World Wide Fund for Nature (WWF), who served as president of the Norwegian chapter for 20 years.
He was such an accomplished sailor, he represented Norway three times at the Olympics.

When Crown Prince Haakon married Mette-Marit in 2001, the king and queen welcomed her four-year-old son from a previous relationship. Høiby was treated as one of the family, but the royal house later stressed that he was never a royal.

The king's daughter Princess Märtha Louise initially married a Norwegian writer before controversially remarrying an American self-styled shaman in 2024. The couple's business activities eventually led to her halting her royal duties.

blocks.caption: Image caption, King Harald welcomed the Norwegian national football team to the palace after they made it to the quarter-finals of the World Cup for the first time this year

blocks.text: Image source, NTB/AFP via Getty Images
King Harald welcomed the Norwegian national football team to the palace after they made it to the quarter-finals of the World Cup for the first time this year

While some Norwegians may have felt Harald was too lenient with his family's controversial life decisions, Vagle believes he had "shown himself to be someone who puts talking things through ahead of issuing harsh instructions".
As the king's health declined, he permanently reduced his public engagements in April 2024.

More recently, he was treated with cortisone for a rare blood condition, haemolytic anaemia, which causes the number of red blood cells in the body to be reduced. He entered hospital on 17 August and his son became regent, assuming his activities.
This year alone the Norwegian royal family has faced compounded personal health challenges and scandals.

The rape trial of Høiby, convicted of multiple offences in June, hung over the royal family for many months. He has now appealed against a four-year jail term and appeared at Harald's bedside shortly before he died.
Days before the trial began, documents were released revealing his mother Mette-Marit's frequent contact with the disgraced financier Jeffrey Epstein.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Harald and Sonja regularly supported Norway's teams at the Olympics

blocks.text: Harald and Sonja regularly supported Norway's teams at the Olympics
She later apologised to Harald and Sonja for her three-year friendship with Epstein and admitted to "poor judgement".
Two days after her son's trial came to an end, Mette-Marit received a lung transplant. She had been diagnosed with a rare form of pulmonary fibrosis eight years prior.
Her doctors will not declare her stable until a year after the transplant, and King Haakon will face a difficult period of succession as he continues to support her.
The crises surrounding the monarchy have had an effect on its popularity. One poll for newspaper Aftenposten found that support had dropped from 72% in 2024 to 54%.

blocks.caption: Family tree of King Haakon's family

blocks.text: Other polls suggested almost half of Norwegians believed Mette-Marit could no longer become queen, although Haakon is now highly likely to say she will.
However, Vagle said criticism was rarely directed at the late king personally, leaving her with the impression that "everyone has loved King Harald".
"When things go wrong in the royal family, people tend to blame anyone but the king," Isaksen remarked.

Haakon has faced questions about the turbulence surrounding his own household that will "follow him into his position as a king", according to Taalesen, however she believes he has shown leadership and dealt with recent events well.
The royal family's main strategy has been to separate itself from Høiby's trial, and Schulsrud-Hansen believes that has largely succeeded.
Although there may be further scrutiny over the Epstein files, the focus for Norwegians now will be on remembering a "greatly beloved king" and supporting his son.

articles.title: Unlocking a 400-year-old mystery in a Nova Scotia marsh
articles.summary: On a river in southwest Nova Scotia, an investigation by a historical sleuth is uncovering long-lost traces of North America’s past.

image.caption: Staff from the Nova Scotia Museum work on a historic dike in Allains River, near the presumed mill site. (Mark Borton)

blocks.text: Nova Scotia
On a river in southwest Nova Scotia, an investigation by a historical sleuth is uncovering long-lost traces of North America’s past.
Poutrincourt gristmill believed to be oldest mill in North America
Allains River (formerly Lequille River) is a winding tributary of the Annapolis River, flowing from the interior of the province to what is now Annapolis Royal.
Four hundred years ago, the river was home to one of the earliest industrial operations established after colonization: a flour mill built in 1607 and destroyed by fire in 1643.

For centuries, the exact location of that mill was a mystery. But now, an amateur historian from the U.S. and a team of researchers and archeologists are getting closer to pinning down its location — shedding light on the history of colonization, contact and millennia of Mi’kmaw presence in Nova Scotia.
“It's a fascinating mystery to solve, and it is a phenomenally important site,” said Mark Borton, a writer from Connecticut who initiated the hunt for the Poutrincourt gristmill.
“An astonishing number of things took place at this location.”
Gristmill needed to produce flour
In 1605, a fortified fur-trade post was built at what Samuel de Champlain called Port Royal, on the Annapolis Basin.
Colonists needed a mill to make flour. “Twenty-five per cent of [French] dietary intake at that time was bread,” said Borton.
The Poutrincourt gristmill — a water-powered mill for grinding grain — appears on maps from the period, including Champlain’s map.

That map caught the eye of Borton, who previously had a career making boating guide books of the East Coast of the United States. Eventually, he retired early and took a trip to the Maritimes in 2018.
That sparked an interest in tidal power and the Bay of Fundy. In researching a book, Borton saw a copy of Champlain’s map, and right away, he knew that the mill was significant.
“What we're looking for is the oldest mill in North America. It's also the beginning of industrial power in North America. So it's an enormous inflection point.”
The problem for Borton — and for generations of historians before him — was that contemporaneous maps did not accurately represent the landscape.
Over the centuries, historians have advanced different theories about where the mill could be.
But Borton believes the mill could be at a location “way outside” historians’ theories.

Taking elements from Champlain’s map and mapping them onto current-day geographical features, Borton was able to narrow down a site. From his home in Connecticut, Borton used Google Maps to look at that location and saw a faint square on the edge of the marsh that could be a foundation.
“You don't get squares in tide marshes unless it's man-made,” he said. “I was thinking, well that's what I'm looking for, where I'm looking for it.”
Borton applied for a permit from the Nova Scotia Museum and continued to investigate.
Area also featured dikes, fishing weir

One clue was that on Champlain’s map, there was a Mi’kmaw fishing weir in the river, opposite the mill. Zooming in on Google Maps, Borton could see a pile of rocks at that spot on the riverbank. “You can't account for the presence of that through natural stream processes.”

Today, the area between the weir and the potential mill site is a marsh, but on Champlain’s map, it’s an island. For Borton, that made sense, since the French could well have diked that part of the river. But there was a hiccup: historical maps did not show any dikes in that area.
Borton approached the Nova Scotia Community College and asked if they would make a lidar map (lidar is a remote sensing method used to make highly accurate 3D maps).
On the resulting maps, Borton could see straight lines and other traces of diking, suggesting a series of dikes dating back to the early 17th century.
This summer, Borton and staff from the Nova Scotia Museum collected samples from the piles of wood and brush that made up the interior of each of those dikes for radiocarbon dating.
“And that's how we move from a good theory to something more solid,” Borton said.
‘A shared landscape’

Borton has also enlisted the help of archeologists at Kwilmu’kw Maw‑klusuaqn — the group tasked with protecting archeological resources by the Assembly of Nova Scotia Mi’kmaw Chiefs — and Saint Mary’s University.

Jonathan Fowler, professor of anthropology at Saint Mary's, said Borton’s project is closely aligned with his team's research on this era, which is consequential as a period of contact and exchange between the French and the Mi’kmaq.
Allains River is an important part of that history, Fowler said.
“In this one place archeologically, you get the European story and European land use, nesting right next to a much older story of human land use: a Mi’kmaw travel corridor and fishing site.”
Fowler’s team is planning to use ground-penetrating radar to further investigate the mill site.

“It's a story of a shared landscape,” Fowler said. “This early period is a period of co-operation. It's a negotiated settlement with Indigenous people. That's interesting, and I think it might hold some lessons for the present and the future.”
Fowler said the project to uncover historical sites on Allains River has itself brought people together, and he commends Borton for being a catalyst.
As for Borton, his investigations have also brought to light a number of other mill sites in the area.
“There are possibly eight national historic sites … in the Allains River, in an area that's only half a kilometre. That’s really extraordinary.”
Borton said as an outsider, it’s not up to him to decide what happens, but he hopes uncovering the truth will make a case for preservation.
“If you think about this as a multicultural landscape, it is Mi’kmaq, it is French-Acadian, it is British … that’s an extraordinary coincidence of activities, so it’s worth preserving.”

articles.title: US judge rules Pentagon's blacklisting of Anthropic unlawful
articles.summary: The AI company was labeled a "supply chain risk" after refusing to allow unrestricted military use of its technology. The judge said "empty invocation of national security is not a blank check" to…

image.caption: Anthropic AI was labeled a 'supply chain risk' by the US government after refusing to allow unrestricted military use of its technologyImage: Jonathan Raa/NurPhoto/picture alliance

blocks.text: A United States federal judge has ruled in favor of the artificial intelligence (AI) company Anthropic in its dispute with the Pentagon over its labeling as a "supply chain risk."

California district judge Rita Lin concluded that the label constituted an attempt by the government to make an example of Anthropic after the company refused to allow unrestricted military use of its technology and criticized the Department of Defense's use of AI.
Lin wrote in a 59-page ruling that "the empty invocation of national security is not a blank check to punish and retaliate against government critics."

She said the government's actions were "based on a desire to make a public example out of Anthropic for its 'arrogance' in criticizing the government, not based on any articulable basis to believe that Anthropic would actually sabotage its model."

An Anthropic spokesperson said they welcomed the judge's ruling, saying in a statement: "We remain focused on working productively with the government to harness AI for our national security so all Americans benefit from this technology."
Anthropic AI: What is the Pentagon dispute all about?

The dispute between the San Francisco-based firm and the government broke out in February when President Donald Trump and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth accused Anthropic of endangering national security after the company declined to allow unrestricted military use of its technology.

"We will not knowingly provide a product that puts America's warfighters and civilians at risk," wrote CEO Dario Amodei in a blog post back in February, adding that AI wasn't reliable enough to be used in fully autonomous weapons systems and expressing concerns over mass surveillance.
Anthropic AI shutdown — Security fears or power play?

In March, the Pentagon designated Anthropic a "supply chain risk" – a highly unusual label to apply to a US firm. The company complained of an "unlawful campaign of retaliation," pointing out that the designation would have negative consequences for its business beyond defense deals.
Indeed, President Trump ordered all US government agencies to stop using Anthropic technology, calling it "a radical left, woke company" and "out-of-control" in a social media rant.
Defense Secretary Hegseth said companies would be expected to cut business links to Anthropic if they wanted to be considered for defense sector deals.
Shortly afterwards, OpenAI, Anthropic's primary tech industry rival and operator of ChatGPT, made its own deal to work with the Pentagon.
Anthropic ruling: What else did Judge Lin say?

In her ruling, Judge Lin, an appointee of former President Joe Biden, wrote that neither the US Constitution nor the federal statute the government invoked allows them to "impose sweeping penalties based principally on Anthropic's critique of the Administration's views."

Earlier in the legal proceedings, Lin had temporarily blocked the Pentagon from labeling the company as a supply chain risk and blocked enforcement of Trump's social media directive ordering all federal agencies to stop using Anthropic and its chatbot Claude.
In a preliminary hearing on July 30, Lin had said that the government's position was "really troubling" and seemed "at odds to me with the First Amendment."
The White House is yet to comment on the decision.

In the coming weeks, Anthropic is expected to launch on the US stock market with an initial public offering (IPO) that could potentially eclipse SpaceX's record Wall Street debut in June, which raised $86 billion (€74 billion).
Why is Anthropic destroying millions of books?
Edited by: Natalie Muller
