articles.title: Norway's King Harald dies at 89
articles.summary: King Harald is succeeded by his son, who has taken the name King Haakon VIII, with Crown Princess Mette-Marit now queen.

image.caption: Prince Harald was born on 21 February 1937Image: Fredrik Varfjell/NTB/AFP

blocks.text: Norway's King Harald, Europe's oldest living monarch, has died at 89, the royal court said on Friday.
The monarch had been receiving treatment for a rare blood condition, hemolytic anemia, at Oslo University Hospital since mid-August.
His son, Prince Haakon automatically becomes King Haakon VIII, with the Norwegian Royal Court also confirming on Thursday that his wife, Mette-Marit, will become queen.
The Norwegian monarch is head of state, but has a largely ceremonial and representative role.
What the palace said about King Harald's death

"It is with deep sadness that we announce that His Majesty King Harald passed away today. King Harald passed away peacefully at Oslo University Hospital on Friday, August 28 at 6:35 a.m.," the palace said in a statement.
Harald's condition worsened over the last few days, and his wife, Queen Sonja, and son, Haakon, canceled all their engagements to be at his bedside.

Harald, who had been king since 1991, suffered a series of health problems in recent years and had increasingly scaled back his official duties. However, he repeatedly ruled out abdicating, saying the oath he had taken on becoming king "lasts for life."

blocks.caption: People gathered for a night vigil at the Palace Square in OsloImage: Odd Andersen/AFP

blocks.text: Hundreds of well-wishers gathered outside the royal palace in Oslo overnight, holding a vigil as the king's condition deteriorated.
King's body moves from hospital to palace
A motor procession carrying King Harald's casket left Oslo University Hospital for the royal palace, as per television images.
Thousands of people have gathered outside the palace to pay their respects to the late king and bid him farewell. They laid down flowers, cards, cuddly toys and Norwegian flags.
"He was the king of the people," mourner Kristoffer Hamre told AFP.
The government has announced a period of national mourning, and flags were flown at half mast on Friday.
"I think he has been such a down-to-earth king who has cared about all of us, and the words he always uses when he gives a speech are so wise and so valuable," Vigdis Haug, 65, told AFP.

blocks.caption: Despite the rain, people queued the streets in wait of King Harald's funeral cortegeImage: Dylan Martinez/REUTERS

blocks.text: Will King Haakon VIII be crowned?

Haakon VIII will take his oath of allegiance to the constitution in a ceremony scheduled for next Tuesday. He is due to deliver a short address that will be broadcast on TV, with parliament saying the address will focus on the monarch's limited power.
Norway no longer stages a traditional coronation.
"King Haakon will promise and swear to govern Norway in accordance with the Constitution and law of the land," President of the Storting [Norway's Parliament], Masud Gharahkhani, said in a statement.

blocks.caption: Representatives of different faiths made their way to the Royal Palace in Oslo to pay their respectsImage: Björn Larsson Rosvall/TT/IMAGO

blocks.text: World leaders, royals pay tribute
Britain's King Charles expressed his condolences for Harald's death, paying tribute to a "towering figure" who guided his country with "warmth and humility."
Norway's prime minister, Jonas Gahr Stoere, said Harald demonstrated an "unwavering faith in the Norwegian people" and "helped us to see the best in ourselves – and in one another."
Swedish King Carl XVI Gustaf said the late king had "been a good friend" and would be "mourned by many in our country."
"I wish my dear Godson Haakon, who now succeeds his father as head of state, success and good fortune in the important role that lies ahead of ‌him," he added.

King Frederik and Queen Mary of Denmark praised Harald's "warm personality and rock-solid calm," saying he "combined duty and responsibility with presence and humanity. He was loved like few others and will be missed by many."

blocks.caption: Flags were flown at half mast at Amalienborg Palace in Denmark following King Harald's deathImage: Ida Marie Odgaard/Ritzau Scanpix/REUTERS

blocks.text: European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen described him as "a true European and a lifelong servant of his people."
"In moments of joy and sorrow, he brought Norwegians together," she said.
NATO chief Mark Rutte said Harald "showed himself to be a dedicated leader. His own military roots made him a champion of the Norwegian military and a long-time friend of NATO."
How will King Harald be remembered?

Born in 1937, Harald became Norway's first prince to be born in the country in more than 500 years. As a child, he fled Norway with his mother and sisters following the Nazi invasion in 1940, spending much of World War II in the United States.

Harald succeeded his father, King Olav V, in January 1991 and went on to modernize the Norwegian monarchy during more than 35 years on the throne. He was widely praised for his response to the 2011 far-right terrorist attacks that killed 77 people and later drew attention for speeches stressing tolerance, diversity and LGBTQ+ equality.
The king's death comes after a turbulent period for Norway's royal family.

blocks.caption: King Harald V waves during a 1991 coronation tour after his accession to the throneImage: Lise Åserud/NTB/picture alliance

blocks.text: Crown Princess [nonw Queen] Mette-Marit has faced scrutiny over her past correspondence with the late US sex offender Jeffrey Epstein. Her son from a previous relationship, Marius Borg Hoiby, was sentenced in June to four years in prison after being convicted of two rapes and dozens of other offenses, including violence against a former partner. He has appealed the verdict.
Edited by: Natalie Muller

articles.title: Trump signs order to rename Lake Ontario as Lake America
articles.summary: Canada has rejected the new name of the lake, which straddles both countries, as their row deepens.

blocks.text: US President Donald Trump has signed an executive order seeking to change the name of Lake Ontario to Lake America.

The move comes after trade talks between the US and Canada collapsed last week, and the US imposed new 50% tariffs on $20bn (C$28bn) worth of Canadian goods. Canada will implement "dollar for dollar" counter-tariffs next month.
Trump said the renaming of the lake, which straddles both countries, was effective immediately. He has broad discretion over how the US recognises landmarks but other countries do not have to follow.
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said in response that "things must be called by their name, and this lake is called Lake Ontario - today and forever".

The executive order gives the US Department of the Interior 30 days to update the name change with the Geographic Names Information Service - the official repository of domestic geographic names in the US.
Carney noted that the name Lake Ontario could be traced back more than 400 years, adding that it preceded the formation of the Canadian Confederation and the US Declaration of Independence.
"We know that the United States is changing," he said. "Their trade relations, their foreign policy, their national monuments, their hydronyms.
"Canadian women and men also know that things must be called by their name, and this lake is called Lake Ontario - today and forever."
There is no universally recognised international body setting the names of international waters.

When Trump took to the White House in 2025, he signed a similar order that changed the Gulf of Mexico to the Gulf of America. Mexico has rejected the name change, arguing a single country cannot rename a shared body of international water.
It also led to a legal dispute between Mexico and tech giant Google, which renamed the gulf in its maps application., external
In that case, Google Maps users in the US see "Gulf of America", while those in Mexico see the "Gulf of Mexico". Those in other countries see the "Gulf of Mexico (Gulf of America)".

The White House at the time also blocked Associated Press reporters from presidential events over the news agency's refusal to adopt the name "Gulf of America" in its coverage. The AP sued the Trump administration in response, and that legal battle is ongoing.
There was a mixed reaction from US politicians.
Trump's Secretary of the Interior Doug Burgum applauded the move, writing: "We're on it, Mr. President!"

"The places and waters that border our nation and support our economy should reflect the greatness of the United States," he said, adding that the US Geological Survey "maps our country for the world to see, and we are PROUD to implement your Executive Order to rename LAKE AMERICA".

But Democratic lawmaker Debbie Dingell of Michigan, the US state that borders four of the five Great Lakes, said that she would introduce a bill in Congress to nullify the name change, calling Trump's order "idiotic".
She wrote: "The Great Lakes are a shared treasure that generations of Americans and Canadians have worked together to protect".
Democratic New York Governor Kathy Hochul said her state, the sole US state bordering Lake Ontario, would not be calling it Lake America.

articles.title: Norway holds its breath as King Harald’s health deteriorates
articles.summary: OSLO, Norway – Norway’s royal family gathered Thursday at King Harald V’s bedside in hospital, while hundreds paid respects outside the palace, after the court announced that the…

blocks.text: OSLO, Norway – Norway’s royal family gathered Thursday at King Harald V’s bedside in hospital, while hundreds paid respects outside the palace, after the court announced that the 89-year-old monarch’s health condition was “extremely serious”.

Queen Sonja and Harald’s 53-year-old son Crown Prince Haakon, who is acting as regent, have cancelled all royal engagements and spent much of Thursday at his side at Oslo University Hospital along with other family members.
The palace said late Thursday afternoon the king’s condition was “unchanged”, shortly after Haakon, his wife Mette-Marit and their two adult children were seen leaving the hospital.
Norwegian broadcaster NRK then on Thursday evening reported that Haakon and Mette-Marit had returned to the hospital a second time.

Europe’s oldest reigning monarch has been in hospital in Oslo since August 17 suffering from haemolytic anaemia, a condition caused by an abnormally rapid destruction of red blood cells which leads to fatigue and shortness of breath.
“His Majesty the King’s health condition is extremely serious,” the palace said, providing no specific details.

Mette-Marit’s son from a previous relationship, Marius Borg Hoiby, who is under house arrest and wearing an ankle bracelet after a rape conviction in June that he has appealed, was also seen leaving the hospital after a more than four-hour visit, as was the king’s sister.
Hundreds of people gathered outside the palace in central Oslo, with many laying down bouquets of flowers for the broadly popular king in front while staying for hours.
“He is Norway’s grandfather,” 57-year-old Trine Bakke Jord told AFP, adding that she appreciated that he was so “down-to-earth” while wiping away tears.
Kaspara Bolstad, 24, told AFP Harald had been “a very steady and warm king”.

“I think the entire Norwegian people see him as a role model and as someone who brings people together. Whether you’re for or against the monarchy, I think he’s well-liked across the board,” she said.
Magnus Skaugseth, 27, agreed, lauding the king’s “inclusive” side.
“When there is so much division and polarization, he was a pillar pointing in the opposite direction.”

Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Store, who cancelled a work trip to Germany on Thursday following the update on the king’s health, told AFP he was “deeply affected” by the news of the king’s health condition.
“I stand together with the entire country as we now send our warmest thoughts to the king and the rest of the royal family,” he said.
Church of Norway bishops also cut short a study visit to Rome where they had met Pope Leo and were to return to Norway Thursday, according to Christian newspaper Vart Land.

Caroline Vagle, a royal reporter for the Se og Hor magazine, called Thursday’s statement from the palace “dramatic”, noting that it was usually “very restrained in its communication about the King’s health, even when he has been hospitalised or undergone treatment.”
“There is also an entire nation that is deeply concerned and saddened. King Harald is a much-loved king,” she told AFP.
The monarch was admitted to Oslo University Hospital due to fluid retention from cortisone treatment he was receiving.
The palace said on Sunday that he was receiving antibiotics for a bacterial infection in his blood and that he had responded to the treatment./dp

articles.title: FM says ‘difficult’ to locate missing Australians in Nepal
articles.summary: SYDNEY, Australia – Australia’s Foreign Minister Penny Wong acknowledged Friday it was “difficult” to locate citizens out of contact in Nepal following deadly flooding. The number…

blocks.caption: An aerial view shows houses lying deluged in sludge after flash floods at Devighat, Bidur Municipality in Nepal’s Nuwakot district on August 27, 2026. Nepal’s disaster agency said that 823 people remained out of contact on August 27, more than 24 hours after a deadly flood tore through the border…

blocks.text: SYDNEY, Australia – Australia’s Foreign Minister Penny Wong acknowledged Friday it was “difficult” to locate citizens out of contact in Nepal following deadly flooding.
The number of Australian nationals missing following the floods has risen to 39, Wong told the Today Show.
“We know many people have been killed, many people are missing and the scale of the disaster is quite horrific,” Wong said.
Australia’s foreign ministry has about 20 people on the ground in Nepal, she said, and will “build on that over the coming days”.
The country will spend Aus$5 million ($3.6 million) on humanitarian assistance for flood relief, she added. /dp

articles.title: Trump orders Lake Ontario to be renamed ‘Lake America’
articles.summary: WASHINGTON, United States — US President Donald Trump stepped up an escalating feud with Canada on Thursday, ordering that Lake Ontario — a body of water shared by both countries — be renamed…

blocks.caption: A Canadian flag flies along the waterfront of Lake Ontario, in Toronto, Ontario, Canada, on August 27, 2026. (Photo by Cole Burston / AFP)

blocks.text: WASHINGTON, United States — US President Donald Trump stepped up an escalating feud with Canada on Thursday, ordering that Lake Ontario — a body of water shared by both countries — be renamed “Lake America.”
Trump signed an executive order on the name change at the White House, further trolling Canada as the North American neighbors plunge deeper into a trade war.
“We’re going to be changing the name of Lake Ontario effective immediately to Lake America,” Trump told reporters in the Oval Office.
Behind Trump’s desk were two maps of the US-Canada border — one with the words “Lake America” in red over the lake, and the other with the header “Making the Great Lakes Even Greater.”
Asked why he was targeting an ally for punishment instead of America’s adversaries, Trump replied: “The Canadian officials have treated us very badly. They’re nasty people.”
“People, oftentimes, they’ll ask me who’s the worst to deal with on trade? And I said that’s easy. Canada. They are the worst to trade with,” the 80-year-old Republican added.

Canada did not immediately comment but is unlikely to accept the renaming of Lake Ontario, the smallest of the five Great Lakes by surface area, which borders Canada’s Ontario province and New York state.
US-Canada trade talks collapsed at the eleventh hour last week, with Trump’s tariffs taking effect on Saturday.
Canada responded with tit-for-tat tariffs on Tuesday, with Prime Minister Mark Carney saying: “You’re at war when you get attacked. We got attacked.”
The same day, Trump announced that he was giving “serious consideration” to changing the name to Lake America.
He then posted a TikTok video late Wednesday saying that he intended to do so after all.
‘Now all we need is an ocean’
The name change mirrors Trump’s unilateral altering of the name of the Gulf of Mexico to the Gulf of America on his first day back in office in January 2025.
That change obliged the US federal government to refer to the gulf by the new designation, although Mexico has rejected any move to rename it and it lacks international recognition.

Trump said the name change was “something I’ve been thinking about for a long time, actually. As you know, we took something called the Gulf of Mexico, we changed it, and now it’s very routinely the Gulf of America.”
Trump also hinted at renaming oceans that border the United States.

“So, if you think about it, we have a gulf, and we have a lake. Now all we need is an ocean. So, maybe we’ll have to change the name of the Atlantic and/or the Pacific. Maybe we’ll change them both,” he said.

While Lake Ontario shares its name with the Canadian province, the name itself is derived from the indigenous Huron word “Ontari’io,” which means “great lake” or “beautiful water,” according to the National Museum of the Great Lakes.
Toronto, Canada’s largest city, sits on its northwestern shore.
During his second presidential term, Trump has irked a series of allies with his outlandish territorial claims, including that Canada should become the 51st US state.
Trump has also laid claim to Greenland, an autonomous territory of NATO ally Denmark, and talked about making Venezuela a state following the US capture of its leader Nicolas Maduro.
In recent days, he has also said that he will make the Strait of Hormuz between Iran and Oman a US territory, despite the fact that the war with Tehran remains ongoing.

articles.title: Himalayan ‘tsunami’: Over 350 dead, 1,400 missing
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — A Filipino was reported to be among the more than a thousand people missing in the flash floods and landslides that occurred on the Nepal-Tibet border, where the confirmed death…

blocks.caption: ENGULFED Surveillance video at a Nepal-China border crossing shows a massive wall of water, mud and debris crashing over a building several stories high on Wednesday morning, engulfing the structure and the entire complex as dozens of people run for their lives below. — CCTV SCREENSHOT VIA AFP

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — A Filipino was reported to be among the more than a thousand people missing in the flash floods and landslides that occurred on the Nepal-Tibet border, where the confirmed death toll had reached at least 359 people as of Thursday.
The lone Filipino was on the initial record cited by the Nepal Tourism Board, though it was yet to be confirmed by the Philippine government at press time.
The tsunami-like rumble of water and mud struck villages and towns on the path of two rivers—Bhote Koshi and Trishuli—on Wednesday night.

A terrifying clip of surveillance video from the Chinese side of the frontier shows a massive wall of mud and debris crashing over a building several stories high on Wednesday morning, engulfing it as dozens of people ran for their lives below.
The surge swept away buses and cars like they were toys.
The US Geological Survey believes the disaster was caused by a glacial collapse that sent a flow of debris engulfing homes along the way.

blocks.caption: SWAMPED Local residents watch as a helicopter flies above houses lying deluged in sludge after flash floods at Devighat, Bidur municipality in Nepal’s Nuwakot district on Aug. 27 —AFP PHOTOS

blocks.text: According to the Nepal Tourism Board, its preliminary record as of 2:45 p.m. on Thursday (Philippine time) showed 644 travelers reported missing in the affected areas, including one Filipino.
The agency gave no further details about the missing Filipino, saying the information was still being verified and crosschecked with travel agencies and other local authorities.

In Manila, the Department of Foreign Affairs (DFA) and the Overseas Workers Welfare Administration (Owwa) have started coordinating with officials in Nepal, as well as with the Filipino community, to determine the extent of the disaster’s impact on Filipinos, Palace press officer Claire Castro said.
Based on information from the DFA and Owwa, there are 128 Filipinos in Nepal, mostly women married to Nepalis. Among them are 18 overseas workers.
President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. on Thursday expressed his condolences to the victims of the disaster.
“The Philippines extends its deepest condolences to our friends in Nepal and to all those affected by the deadly flash flood yesterday,” Mr. Marcos said in a social media post.
“Our deepest sympathies go out to those who lost family, loved ones, and friends. Please accept our most heartfelt prayers for strength in this difficult time,” he added.
Wall of mud, debris

blocks.caption: Aerial views show houses inundated by mud and water in Nuwakot district—AFP PHOTOS

blocks.text: The Nepali police on Thursday said they had recovered 162 bodies, as rescue teams rushed to find more than 1,400 people still missing.
Another 823 people, including 579 Nepali and foreign tourists, remained out of contact in Nepal, according to the country’s disaster agency.
Across the border, Chinese state media said the “mudslide disaster” at the Gyirong Port in Tibet claimed three lives while 558 people, including 260 foreigners, were still missing.
Raju Bhadel, 56, a businessman in Nepal’s Nuwakot district, recounted receiving a call from his brother-in-law in distress.
“They were crying and said their entire house had been swept away. Three family members were rescued, but his brother is still missing,” he said.
Also at Nuwakot, teacher Manok Mishra witnessed “nine trucks being swept away by the floods, including people.”

blocks.caption: Aerial views show houses inundated by mud and water in Nuwakot district—AFP PHOTOS

blocks.text: ‘Inland tsunami’
Rescuers waded through mud and sludge to look for survivors after floodwaters buried the lower floors of multistory buildings.
The foreigners out of contact included Indians, and others from Australia, Britain, Malaysia, the Netherlands, Portugal, South Africa, South Korea, and the United States, Nepal’s tourism board said.
Hiking company Himalayan Glacier told Agence France-Presse (AFP) 47 people from a group including two children were missing in Nepal.

The sudden rush of mud and debris was “like an inland tsunami, traveling nearly 170 kilometers down the Bhote Koshi valley into Central Nepal,” said environmental historian Ruth Gamble of La Trobe University in Australia.
“It is a popular route for international tourists traveling from Kathmandu to Lhasa,” she added.

blocks.caption: GRIEF A girl cries as she waits for news of relatives missing after flash floods in Bidur, Nepal, on Aug. 27. —AP

blocks.text: Rasuwa, in the north of Nepal, was the first district to be affected. But deaths have been reported from seven Nepali districts in total as the floodwaters raged through to Chitwan in the south, on the border with India.
The Nepali Army was carrying out flights and had rescued scores of people, while others living near the river in danger zones had been told to relocate.
Tibet government officials mobilized nearly 800 emergency workers and 150 vehicles as well as sniffer dogs and speed boats to help the rescue efforts, China’s state-run news agency Xinhua said.
The International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies said it was dispatching emergency supplies including blankets, first aid kits, stretchers, and body bags.
Seismic event

blocks.caption: Himalayan ‘tsunami’: Over 350 dead, 1.4K missing

blocks.text: The cause of the disaster was not immediately clear in the hours after it occurred early Wednesday, but the US Geological Survey said it was a glacial collapse that caused seismic activity and the “catastrophic” downstream impacts in Nepal and Tibet.
“This event was initially reported as a magnitude 4.4 earthquake,” it said.

“Additional analysis of nearby seismic stations, long period seismic waves, and satellite imagery led to the determination that the seismic event was instead a glacial collapse and debris flow, and that no earthquake had occurred.”
Climate change is causing glaciers to melt worldwide, increasing the risks of glacial lake floods and glacial collapses.
Qianggong Zhang, head of climate and environmental risks at the Kathmandu-based International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development, warned of the potential for a second flood.
“With a blockage still lodged upstream on the Nepal-China border river, authorities warn a second flood may occur,” he told AFP. —With a report from AFP

articles.title: UN body calls for release of Cumpio, activists from arbitrary detention
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — Human rights group Karapatan on Wednesday welcomed the findings of the United Nations Working Group on Arbitrary Detention (UN WGAD), which declared as arbitrary the detention…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — Human rights group Karapatan on Wednesday welcomed the findings of the United Nations Working Group on Arbitrary Detention (UN WGAD), which declared as arbitrary the detention of Tacloban community journalist Frenchie Mae Cumpio, humanitarian worker Marielle Domequil and human rights worker Alexander Abinguña.
The UN WGAD stated its findings in its opinion report, which was released only recently and first adopted during its 105th session held from March 23 to April 1.

“The UN WGAD opinions reaffirm our position that the charges against Cumpio, Domequil and Abinguña are baseless and trumped-up, that their rights under the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights were violated, and that their release from prison is long overdue,” Karapatan secretary general Cristina Palabay said in a statement.
The rights groups called for the release of the three, noting that they have been detained for more than six years following their arrest on Feb. 7, 2020.
Terrorism financing

Cumpio and Domequil were convicted in January by the Tacloban City Regional Trial Court for “terrorism financing” and sentenced to 12 to 18 years in prison. From the Tacloban City Jail, they were transferred in April to the Correctional Institute for Women in Mandaluyong City where they remain detained after their petition for bail was denied by the court. They have appealed their conviction before the Court of Appeals.

“The inordinate delay of the court proceedings that has prolonged their detention is an additional layer of injustice against the three. Their release should immediately be given due course,” Palabay said.
The UN WGAD found a lack of factual and legal basis for the criminal charges against the three, concluding that their deprivation of liberty was arbitrary.
It also determined that their detention stemmed from the exercise of their rights to freedom of expression, peaceful assembly and association.
Based on the UN body’s report, the three have been targets of Red-tagging and accused of associating with the Communist Party of the Philippines and its armed wing, the New People’s Army.
It said the appropriate remedy would be the immediate release of Cumpio, Domequil and Abinguña, along with an enforceable right to compensation and other forms of reparation under international law.
Probe pushed

The UN WGAD also called for a full and independent investigation into the circumstances surrounding their arbitrary detention as it urged authorities to hold accountable those responsible for violating their rights.

In June, United Nations Special Rapporteur Irene Khan cautioned that freedom of expression is “under attack in multiple ways,” citing the case of Cumpio in her final report to the UN Human Rights Council. —WITH A REPORT FROM SHERIDAN DELFINO

articles.title: Iran, Qatar hold Hormuz talks as US blockade chokes Iran’s oil imports
articles.summary: TEHRAN, Iran — Iran’s top diplomat met his Qatari counterpart on Thursday in Tehran for talks on the strategic Strait of Hormuz, as a US naval blockade squeezes oil supplies to Iran amid a…

blocks.caption: Before the Iran war, the Strait of Hormuz carried around 20% of global crude exports from the Persian Gulf. Image: REUTERS

blocks.text: TEHRAN, Iran — Iran’s top diplomat met his Qatari counterpart on Thursday in Tehran for talks on the strategic Strait of Hormuz, as a US naval blockade squeezes oil supplies to Iran amid a domestic shortfall.

The visit by Qatar’s Foreign Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al Thani follows a week of intense diplomacy in Iran involving separate meetings with Oman’s top diplomat and senior Pakistani officials seeking ways to end the Middle East war and reopen Hormuz.

It also comes as Washington threatens wider secondary sanctions against countries, banks and companies that continue doing business with Iran, part of a broader campaign it has called “economic asphyxiation.”
Iranian state television said Al Thani, who is also Qatar’s prime minister, had met with Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi, without providing details.
In a statement after the talks, Al Thani said they focused on efforts to de-escalate tensions and boost security in the region.
“Qatar believes that dialogue and diplomacy remain the best way to overcome crises,” he wrote on X.
Qatar’s foreign ministry said they discussed the proposed framework for Hormuz between Iran and Oman.
“Talks stressed the importance of respecting freedom of navigation in the Strait of Hormuz in accordance with international law,” Al Thani added.
Alongside mediator Pakistan, Qatar had played a key role in securing an April ceasefire and June deal between Iran and the United States, but those deals have since collapsed.
Fuel shortage

Since war with the United States broke out on February 28, Iran has maintained tight control over Hormuz, a vital global energy conduit, with Washington imposing a naval counter-blockade on Iranian ports.
On Wednesday, Iran’s Vice President Mohammad Jafar Ghaempanah said the blockade had prevented his country from importing enough gasoline to cover a shortfall in domestic production.
“Gasoline production is insufficient, and because of the US naval blockade, we cannot import it,” he was quoted by the official IRNA news agency as saying.
In recent days, many Iranians have been seen queuing outside gas stations. Presidential chief of staff Mohsen Haji-Mirzaei said gasoline quotas would be reviewed, without elaborating.
Iran, a major oil producer with some of the world’s cheapest fuel, has for years heavily subsidized gasoline, making changes to pricing politically sensitive.
As the US seeks to strangle Iran’s economy, Iranian officials have dismissed the measures as “failed policies” that will not force Tehran to change course.
“The country is in an all-out economic war,” said Iran’s top negotiator Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf in a statement carried by local media.
“We will see that the government … will defeat the enemy on this ground as well,” he added.
Even before the war, Iran’s economy was battered by decades of international sanctions and has long suffered from chronic inflation and a weakening currency.
Talks on Hormuz

Iran has for weeks been in talks with Oman, which also overlooks the Strait of Hormuz, over a framework agreement that would establish a “temporary corridor” for shipping and provide for clearing mines Tehran says were laid during the war.
Iran’s Revolutionary Guards on Wednesday said the two countries had agreed on each country’s share of the waters and any revenues collected from managing the waterway.

Tehran has nonetheless insisted that the strait will not be reopened unless Washington meets its demands, including lifting its naval blockade, unfreezing Iranian assets abroad and removing oil sanctions.
Since the war broke out, Iranian forces have required vessels to obtain permission to transit the waterway and struck ships that failed to comply.
Tehran has also sought to impose service fees on ships using the strait — a move strongly opposed by Washington and regional countries.
On Thursday, the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations said an “unknown projectile” had struck a tanker in Hormuz this week, causing a fire that was later extinguished.

articles.title: Alex Eala, Iva Jovic share court with dads in US Open exhibition
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines —Alex Eala fell to close friend Iva Jovic, 6-3, in the Stars of the Open exhibition on Friday morning, but both enjoyed a lighthearted tuneup ahead of the US Open. Towards the end…

blocks.text: Alexandra Eala of the Philippines embraces her father during the stars of the open at Fan Week as part of the 2026 US Open at USTA Billie Jean King National Tennis Center on August 27, 2026 in New York City. Caleb Bowlin/Getty Images/AFP
MANILA, Philippines —Alex Eala fell to close friend Iva Jovic, 6-3, in the Stars of the Open exhibition on Friday morning, but both enjoyed a lighthearted tuneup ahead of the US Open.
Towards the end of the match, the two rising stars brought their fathers onto the court for a brief mixed doubles match, ending the exhibition with a heartwarming moment and a hug with their dads.
A father-daughter moment to remember 💙 Alexandra Eala and Iva Jovic bring their dads on court for a little friendly competition. pic.twitter.com/JGfvPZM9rv — US Open Tennis (@usopen) August 28, 2026
Eala and Jovic also exchanged messages in their native languages, addressing the crowd at a packed Arthur Ashe Stadium in Flushing Meadows.
Eala fought back from a 0-2 deficit to tie the one-set match at 3-all, but Jovic won the final three games to finish the exhibition in less than an hour.

blocks.caption: Iva Jovic of the United States embraces her father during the stars of the open at Fan Week as part of the 2026 US Open at USTA Billie Jean King National Tennis Center on August 27, 2026 in New York City

blocks.text: Iva Jovic of the United States embraces her father during the stars of the open at Fan Week as part of the 2026 US Open at USTA Billie Jean King National Tennis Center on August 27, 2026 in New York City. Caleb Bowlin/Getty Images/AFP (Photo by Caleb Bowlin / GETTY IMAGES NORTH AMERICA / Getty Images via AFP)
Jovic has now beaten Eala three times this year, including at the French Open and HSBC Championships.
Proceeds from Stars of the Open will go to the USTA Foundation.
Eala, seeded 17th in the US Open, will face a qualifier in the first round. Should she advance, she will meet the winner between Oleksandra Oliynykova and wild card Reese Brantmeier.
Eala could face No. 14 seed Jovic in the third round. The American opens against Magdalena Fręch, with the winner facing Magda Linette or another qualifier in the second round.

articles.title: Nepal floods: Survivors, swallowed by silt, recount horror
articles.summary: BIDUR, Nepal —Survivors from Nepal’s flood-ravaged districts, some on stretchers, others gently supported by the shoulders, were airlifted to safety on Thursday as the constant roar of…

blocks.caption: This frame grab taken from video released by the Armed Police Force of Nepal on August 26, 2026 shows rescue workers carrying a person after massive floods and landslides in Rasuwa. Rescue teams rushed on August 27 to find hundreds of people missing on the Nepal-Tibet border in flash floods and l…

blocks.text: BIDUR, Nepal —Survivors from Nepal’s flood-ravaged districts, some on stretchers, others gently supported by the shoulders, were airlifted to safety on Thursday as the constant roar of helicopters echoed across the devastated town of Bidur.
A few walked alone, their faces frozen in shock, as helicopters landed every few minutes on a football field inside the town’s military cantonment, whipping up clouds of dust.
Among the survivors was customs agent Omkar Joshi, who spent the previous night stranded on a hilltop in the border town of Timure before being rescued.
“Everything is finished,” Joshi, 35, told AFP, his voice breaking with emotion.
The town he fled had all but vanished beneath a torrent of water, mud and debris.
“Ninety percent” of its people were dead, he said, swallowed by silt.
“It is a giant graveyard. All that is left are sand and pebbles, soaked red by human blood.”
He said hundreds of people survived only by scrambling up nearby slopes as floodwaters roared through the valley below.
“It rained all night, but we stayed put till the choppers came for us,” he added.

On Wednesday, a tsunami-like wall of water and mud swept through villages and towns along Nepal’s Bhote Koshi and Trishuli rivers. Nepali police have recovered 270 bodies, but search operations continue.
Many of the missing are foreign tourists caught in the disaster, which according to the US Geological Survey was caused by a glacial collapse that resulted in an overwhelming flow of icy debris.
Buried alive
In Bidur, scores of anxious relatives peered through the barbed wire separating the football ground from the road, hoping to see the familiar face of a loved one.
Sita BK was searching for her younger brother Ramchandra, a schoolteacher in Timure.
“I spoke to him in the morning just before I heard the news,” said the 37-year-old. “But ever since, his phone is switched off.”
She said she had no choice but to wait.
“They (officials) said their first priority is to rescue people who are contactable,” she said. “But my brother is not.”
Nearby, Anisha Nepali sat quietly in a corner, tears running down her cheeks.
The 24-year-old had rushed back from Kathmandu on Wednesday after hearing about the disaster, but has received no news of her missing mother and younger brother.
“I have given their names, but am yet to hear anything,” she said.

Two young girls climbed out of a helicopter, still in their bright green school uniforms. A rescuer gently caressed their heads and offered them biscuits and water, before leading them away to safety.
Farther downstream, the devastation was etched into the shattered landscape of Devighat.
Residents said only one of roughly 150 houses along the banks of the Trishuli River remained intact: a four-storey old-age care home.
But rescuers said up to seven elderly residents were buried when a landslide crashed into the home as they tried to flee.
Images shared by a rescuer showed one of the victims trapped beneath an uprooted tree.
Sabir Miyan, a resident of the town, said warnings that floodwaters were racing down from the mountains had helped save lives.
“Many of us could save our lives but everything else is gone,” he said. “It is all ruins now.”

articles.title: Philippines posts highest estimated adolescent HIV incidence in Asean
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — The Philippines has gone from having one of the lowest estimated rates of new HIV infections among adolescents in Southeast Asia in 2000 to recording the region’s highest…

blocks.caption: Composite image from INQUIRER File photo

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — The Philippines has gone from having one of the lowest estimated rates of new HIV infections among adolescents in Southeast Asia in 2000 to recording the region’s highest estimated incidence in 2025, according to newly released Unicef data.

The estimated incidence of new HIV infections among Filipinos ages 15 to 19 reached 0.49 per 1,000 uninfected adolescents in 2025, up from below 0.01 per 1,000 in 2000, based on Unicef’s Key HIV epidemiology indicators for children and adolescents aged 0–19, 2000–2025.

The figures were analyzed by University of the Philippines Diliman associate professor and Inquirer data scientist Dr. Rogelio Alicor Panao, who noted that the Philippines’ trajectory was markedly different from those of several Southeast Asian countries that started with higher estimated adolescent HIV incidence.
“Twenty-five years ago, the Philippines was among the Southeast Asian countries least affected by HIV among adolescents. Today, it has the region’s highest estimated incidence,” Panao said.
“Put another way, that is about 49 new infections for every 100,000 uninfected adolescents in a year, or roughly one for every 2,000,” he added.
As a rough illustration of the rate, Panao noted that in a high school with about 10,000 students, it would correspond to around five new infections in a year.
From one of the lowest to the highest

Unicef data showed that the Philippines had an estimated adolescent HIV incidence of below 0.01 per 1,000 in 2000. Its estimated rate then rose to 0.10 in 2011, 0.25 in 2019 and 0.49 in 2025, according to Panao.
“Interestingly, countries in ASEAN that started much worse have gone in the opposite direction,” Panao said.

blocks.caption: inqmetrics

blocks.text: Thailand, for instance, reduced its estimated incidence from 1.80 per 1,000 in 2000 to 0.29 in 2025. Myanmar brought its rate down from 1.26 to 0.43, while Cambodia reduced its estimate from 0.68 to 0.16.
Panao described the contrast as significant because the Philippines started with a much smaller estimated adolescent HIV problem than those countries.
“Twenty-five years ago, the Philippines was among the Southeast Asian countries least affected by HIV among adolescents. Today, it has the region’s highest estimated incidence,” he said.
Philippines has taken steps
Still, Panao noted that the Philippines has introduced measures aimed at improving HIV prevention and access to testing.
Under Republic Act No. 11166, the age of consent for voluntary HIV testing was lowered to 15. The Philippines has also added pre-exposure prophylaxis, or PrEP, to the Philippine National Formulary.
Comprehensive sexuality education has likewise been expanded.
However, Panao said implementation remains uneven “due to local resistance, cultural taboos and other institutional bottlenecks.”
Prevention needs to reach young people
Panao said the rise in estimated incidence calls for consideration of measures that could make HIV prevention and testing more accessible to adolescents.

“[M]aybe it is time to give serious thought to expanding confidential, routine HIV testing beyond traditional clinics; ensuring consistent access to condoms, PrEP and HIV self-testing; strengthening comprehensive sexuality education; and bringing youth-focused prevention into the spaces where young people actually seek information and support, including online platforms,” he said.
He said the experience of other countries in the region shows that high adolescent HIV incidence is not necessarily irreversible.
“Thailand, Myanmar and Cambodia have shown that high adolescent HIV incidence can be pushed down,” Panao said.
“The Philippines began with a much smaller problem. It now stands to face a much bigger one,” he added.

articles.title: From deliveries to data: How Ninja Van is rewiring business operations with FieldSight
articles.summary: Every day, thousands of Ninja Van riders weave through streets and barangays nationwide. They know every corner shop, sari-sari store, and neighborhood grocery store on their routes. But what if they…

blocks.text: Every day, thousands of Ninja Van riders weave through streets and barangays nationwide. They know every corner shop, sari-sari store, and neighborhood grocery store on their routes.

blocks.caption: Ninja Van FieldSight

blocks.text: But what if they could do more than move parcels? With an extensive network and a trained fleet of riders, they could also provide brands with real-time visibility into what is actually happening on store shelves—whether products are in stock, displayed correctly, or losing space to competitors.

This is the idea behind Ninja Van’s newest operational engine, Ninja FieldSight, an AI-powered, real-time retail intelligence solution. Combining Ninja Van’s delivery footprint with computer vision and analytics, FieldSight enables FMCG brands to monitor product availability, verify retail execution, and track competitor activity – without the high costs, heavy retainers, and long lag times of traditional market research agencies
Addressing the FMCG Blind Spot

blocks.caption: Ninja Van FieldSight

blocks.text: High-priority retail doors and neighborhood stores account for a significant share of everyday consumer purchases. Yet, even across an FMCG brand’s most critical store locations, a blind spot persists: a lack of continuous, real-time visibility into what actually happens on the shelf between delivery runs. Out-of-stock products go unnoticed, promotional displays are improperly executed, or competitors gain shelf space, long before brands become aware.

“The future of FMCG retail success is no longer just about making sure packages are being delivered to the stores. It’s also about understanding what happens on the shelf once they get there,” says Danielle Hung, Head of Business Planning & Operations, Ninja Van.

Traditional field audits have long been used to bridge this gap, but they come with high overhead costs, prolonged recruitment, and tedious deployment cycles. Brands are left waiting during long report turnaround times, with no ability to view their data while still fresh. “Long data lead times deliver yesterday’s news weeks too late. By the time insights reach decision-makers, the information is often already outdated,” Hung noted.
Reinforcing Delivery Network with Data

Instead of building a separate field force, Ninja Van leveraged something it already had: one of the country’s largest logistics networks. FieldSight builds on its B2C and B2B delivery infrastructure, with thousands of Ninja Van riders plying the roads daily.

As riders pass target retail touchpoints, FieldSight automatically prompts them to capture shelf images through a proprietary AI bot on their phones. Uploaded photos are instantly processed by Vision AI to validate that they are high-resolution, accurately labeled, and backed by geo-tagged, time-stamped visual proof.

“We don’t send temporary auditors into unfamiliar streets,” Hung added. “Our riders are already part of their neighborhood’s daily rhythm. That allows us to collect retail intelligence naturally as part of our existing operations”
Faster Insights, Deeper Reach, Real-Time Deployment

blocks.caption: Ninja Van FieldSight

blocks.text: FieldSight gives FMCG brands strategic advantages in terms of speed, reach, accuracy, and flexibility, shifting retail strategy from reactive troubleshooting to proactive shelf management.

Because touchpoints are identified based on rider proximity and data is transmitted immediately, SKU availability can be confirmed in near real time. This replaces weeks-long report cycles with daily feedback loops, ensuring they can respond with timely corrective action. Through automated shelf-share measurement, live dashboards and interactive heat maps, brands can reduce stock-outs, improve on-shelf availability, protect promotional investments and respond more quickly to competitor activity.

While traditional audits provide market intelligence through slow, manual reporting cycles, FieldSight ensures ground-level data is accessible. Brands gain a real-time window to competitor pulse, including rival pricing, neighborhood promotions, and new product launches.

Moreover, every audit is backed by high-resolution, geo-tagged, and time-stamped visual verification, creating a reliable audit trail that confirms shelf placement and planogram compliance. Unlike manual self-reporting—where data can be altered, misattributed, or delayed—FieldSight is designed to eliminate human error, field fraud, and blind spots.

Whether conducting a rapid hyper-local spot check or a coordinated nationwide audit, FieldSight scales to business needs. Brands can launch customized campaigns across selected territories or simultaneously nationwide, with as little as 24 hours’ notice and no lengthy recruitment or deployment period.
Winning at the Counter: From Data to Brand Impact

By combining historical audit data with real-time shelf insights from FieldSight, brand managers can anticipate supply gaps and intervene before empty shelves compromise brand trust, erode customer loyalty, and drive shoppers to competitors.

True brand impact happens when products remain reliably within arm’s reach at the exact moment of purchase. FieldSight extends visibility beyond logistics, giving brands confidence not only that products have reached their destinations, but that they are present, visible, and retail-ready on store shelves.

Powered by its nationwide delivery network and advanced AI, Ninja Van is redefining operational excellence—transforming everyday deliveries into real-time retail intelligence that drives stronger execution and better business outcomes.
Your product left the warehouse. But is it actually on the shelf? FieldSight turns your delivery footprint into real-time retail intelligence as they happen.

articles.title: About 90 Americans unaccounted for in Nepal-Tibet catastrophic floods
articles.summary: McMINNVILLE, Tenn — US officials said about 90 American citizens remained unaccounted for Thursday, a day after catastrophic flash floods engulfed a border area of China and Nepal, killing hundreds…

blocks.caption: A government helicopter conducts a rescue mission amidst the devastation left by flash flooding in Nepal’s Nuwakot district, Thursday, Aug. 27, 2026. (AP Photo/Rajesh Kumar Singh)

blocks.text: McMINNVILLE, Tenn — US officials said about 90 American citizens remained unaccounted for Thursday, a day after catastrophic flash floods engulfed a border area of China and Nepal, killing hundreds of people. A spiritual organization said that 22 Americans associated with it were unaccounted for.
In a statement, the US State Department said it is not aware of any US deaths, but three Americans have been rescued.
Many of the missing were on a pilgrimage to Mount Kailash in Tibet, a sacred site for Hindus, Buddhists and others.

Social media posts were surfacing Thursday from loved ones pleading for people to provide updates or circulate information about Americans they had lost contact with — a Virginia woman traveling with a tour group, a Texas couple on a birthday trip and a mother accompanying her 14-year-old daughter.
Among those on a guided tour was Venus Rajnikant Patel, a 45-year-old Indian-born US citizen who recently moved from St. Louis to Cincinnati to help his family.

Patel’s brother, Dennis, said Venus called him and their parents a few hours before the floods, showing them his hotel room on the Nepalese side of the border and talking about how excited he was to cross into Tibet. He had been planning the pilgrimage for two years, his brother said.

Another American who is missing is 72-year-old Jitendra Patel, a Long Island resident who was with a tour group on a Hindu pilgrimage to Mount Kailash, according to his son, Sunny Patel. Jitendra last called Wednesday morning local time on WhatsApp to say that he had crossed the border into Tibet.

When Sunny first saw video of the flooding he thought no one could survive it, Sunny said. He then contacted his mother to ask about his father’s whereabouts. His mother said Jitendra was in the exact same area as the flooding.
“My heart sank,” Sunny said, adding that he “didn’t think it was possible that my dad would be there at ground zero.”
“It gets worse by every hour, obviously,” he added.

Indian spiritual guru Jaggi Vasudev, also known as Sadhguru, said in a post on X that 77 people returning from Mount Kailash with groups organized by his Isha Foundation were at an immigration center in Gyirong, Tibet, when the floods struck.

Leslie Crespi, a community liaison for the foundation’s US campus, said that 22 of them were Americans affiliated with the foundation and that three volunteers supporting the trekkers were also at the immigration center when the floods hit.
“We had communication with the coordinator of the group at about 9:05 Nepalese time saying that they had arrived there. And then by 9:14 is when this flash flood hit,” Crespi said.

The Isha Foundation is a spiritual organization based in India and its US campus, the Isha Institute of Inner-sciences, is a yoga and meditation retreat center located in the mountains near McMinnville, Tennessee.

At a candlelight vigil in New York City on Thursday, Tak Ruwali, a Long Island resident who is from one of the Nepalese districts affected by the flooding, said that he is talking with people in Nepal and many regional tourist guides are “out of contact now.”
“It means they are probably gone,” Ruwali added.
Talking to reporters in the Oval Office on Thursday, President Donald Trump said US officials have spoken with Nepalese leaders and offered to provide “anything they want.”
Trump said there were 50 or 60 Americans in the area but added that a full accounting hasn’t been completed./dp

articles.title: ‘Confluence of errors’ led to Belgian tourist Celine Cremer’s death in Tasmanian wilderness, coroner finds
articles.summary: Coroner finds 31-year-old deviated from a walking track as dusk fell, four days before the winter solstice

blocks.text: Overlapping errors, including a lack of preparation in near-freezing winter weather, contributed to the death of a Belgian tourist on a wilderness track.
Celine Cremer set off on a walk at Philosopher Falls in Tasmania’s remote north-west on 17 June 2023 and was reported missing almost 10 days later.
Extensive initial police efforts found no trace of the 31-year-old before private searches organised by her friends and family discovered her remains near a river in January 2026.
In findings published on Friday, the coroner, Madeleine Wilson, ruled Cremer died between 17 and 21 June, 2023 as a result of an accident.
Her death followed a “confluence of errors” that began when she took a walking track towards Magnet Dam after visiting the Philosopher Falls lookout.
“The track to Magnet Dam was not well defined and she wandered off track and became lost,” Wilson said.
“The deviation from the track occurred late in the day, four days before the winter solstice, at which time the afternoon light was starting to fade.”

blocks.caption: Searchers scoured wilderness in 2023 near the Philosopher Falls track in Tasmania in the hunt for Cremer. Her remains were found earlier this year. Photograph: Tasmania police

blocks.text: Overnight temperatures in the area at the time were close to freezing and Cremer had insufficient clothing, including nothing waterproof, Wilson said.
Phone reception was intermittent and she lost her mobile, which was her only form of communication, late in the afternoon on the day she set out.
Her phone was found by a search party of volunteers in December 2025.
Recovered data showed she took several photos and videos between 2.21pm and 2.42pm and used Google maps several times afterwards with the last input recorded at 4.18pm.
It is likely Cremer got lost around 3.49pm and subsequently became disorientated without her phone and mistakenly changed direction, the coroner said.
“It is not possible to determine the route taken once Cremer lost her mobile phone, to her final resting place in the Arthur River,” Wilson said.
It was possible Cremer slipped and fell, or tried unsuccessfully to cross the river.
Cremer had travelled to Australia in 2022 on a working holiday and was planning to return to the mainland four days after the Philosopher Falls walk.
after newsletter promotion
Wilson praised the efforts of a private search company and volunteers which ultimately led to the first discovery of Cremer’s remains.
The police response to the missing person report was appropriate and their search efforts were guided by “accepted methodologies”.
Police efforts were somewhat limited by weather, Wilson said, noting water levels in the Arthur River were significantly higher in 2023 than when her remains were found.

blocks.caption: The car of then-missing Belgian tourist Celine Cremer in northwest Tasmania in 2023. Photograph: Tasmania police/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: Tasmania Police has committed to a review into the use of private search groups in missing persons investigations, including consideration of formal protocols.
Cremer failed to follow standard safety precautions, such as taking appropriate equipment and telling people where you are going, Wilson said.
“Walkers should familiarise themselves with these standard safety messages before embarking on short walks, day walks or multi-day hikes,” she said.
“Walkers should also be aware that mobile coverage is often intermittent or unavailable in remote areas of the Tasmanian wilderness and should plan accordingly.”

Wilson recommended the local council put up signs at the entrance to the Philosopher Falls track, explaining it is not managed for recreational use and the surface is degraded, uneven and may be hazardous.

articles.title: Celeste Legaspi says she's 'not so crazy about BINI,' draws varied reactions

The veteran singer-actress shared her thoughts on the two groups when asked about her take on the state of the music industry, during an interview vlog for “Senior Moments with Louie Montalbo” last May.

“I like the SB19 a lot. They are really, really good. I’m not so crazy about the BINI kasi parang… Hindi sila masyadong… Anyway…,” Legaspi said, opting not to continue her statement. “SB19—they’re really, really good. I’m so proud of them when I see them next to the Koreans.”
